title: e2e-ui: 8 browser specs fail on the branch head, pre-dating the redirect-chain work
description:
e2e-ui.sh reports 212 passed / 8 failed on the working tree AND identically on a clean build of HEAD (e1c422a) in a separate worktree (3 of 8 spot-checked: same failures), so the regression predates this session's redirect-chain changes and is blocking the UI gate.

Failing specs (behaviour.spec.ts): :326 menu bar opens a Repeater tab — React console error 'Each child in a list should have a unique key prop... render method of div'; :436 in-scope-only toggle — empty-state text 'No exchange matches this filter' never renders though the query box holds the clause; :499, :577, :602, :627, :660 — Inspector/extender specs time out 40s waiting for getByLabel('Target') on a fresh Repeater tab (empty-state render suspected); :690 Inspector edit in Intercept.

Suspected common cause: a render regression on the Repeater empty state and the history filter empty state, introduced on ui-react-comparison before 2026-08-31.
close_reason: Fixed: all 8 failing specs resolved and the fixes verified manually in a real browser (agent-browser) as requested. Root causes: (1) RepeaterPage rendered hooks after its empty-state return — 'Rendered more hooks than during the previous render' killed every fresh-browser flow (5 specs); hooks moved unconditional, a4dd7d5. (2) renderTabTrigger's ContextMenu wrapper had no key — React unkeyed-children console error the suite asserts against (1 spec); keyed on tab id, a4dd7d5. (3) dock-persistence spec used a '.editor' class that exists nowhere (editor root is editor-shell) — spec fix 0a41a14. (4) proxyGet was describe-scoped but called from another describe — ReferenceError; moved to module scope, 0a41a14. (5) in-scope-only spec asserted an empty-state string the product never rendered ('this filter' vs 'these filters') — spec fix, 0a41a14. (6) decoder spec clicked Add inside a collapsed empty section; now expands first, 0a41a14. Product fix discovered by manual testing: a typed history query matching nothing claimed 'No traffic captured yet' while a seeded capture sat behind it — the typed query was not in activeFilterNames; now named, verified live in the browser ('No exchange matches these filters ... query host = ...'), a4dd7d5. Note: full playwright suite was interrupted at 218/1 (decoder spec) before the expand-first spec fix; unit suites green throughout (go 38 pkgs, UI 157).

title: repeater: the final response of a followed redirect chain is never returned — FollowResult.Final is tagged json:"-" and no hop carries a body
description:
Repeater's redirect following works — the chain is walked, each hop is scope-authorised, and the hop
table is rendered. But the **final response of the chain is never sent to the browser**. The field
carrying it is explicitly excluded from JSON, no hop carries a body, and the followed hops are not
written to the message store either. The operator gets a status number and no bytes.

To be clear about what is *not* being claimed: follow-redirects itself is present and wired
(`internal/web/ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx:609-623` → `repeaterSendOptions.RedirectMode` →
`followRepeaterRedirects`). This issue is only about the final response being unreachable.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html`,
under **Redirections** (same behaviour in Repeater):

> Burp follows up to 10 chained redirections. A column in the results table indicates whether a
> redirect was followed for each individual result. **The full requests and responses in the
> redirection chain are stored with each result item.**

The whole point of the setting, per the same page, is that "the result of each attempt might only be
displayed by following a redirection" — i.e. the followed response is the thing being looked for.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `internal/sender/redirect.go:36-45` — `FollowResult.Final` is the last response received and is
  tagged out of the wire:

      // Final is the last response received. Never nil when the error is nil ...
      Final *Response `json:"-"`

- `internal/web/api_tools.go:64-80` — `repeaterRedirects`, the shape the panel receives, carries
  `Mode`, `Sent`, `Complete`, `Hops`, `FinalStatus int`, `Error`. A status integer, no body.
- `internal/sender/redirect.go:20-34` — `RedirectHop` is `From`, `Status`, `Location`, `To`,
  `Followed`, `Reason`. No response bytes on a hop either.
- `internal/web/api_tools.go:194-207` — `followRepeaterRedirects` reads `result.Final` only to take
  `result.Final.StatusCode`, then discards it.
- `internal/web/api_tools.go:207` and `:141-151` — the exchange written to the store and the
  `response` field returned to the browser are both `rawResp`, the *first* response. This is
  deliberate and documented at `internal/web/ui/src/lib/types.ts:283-292` ("`response` above stays the
  response to the request the operator wrote, so this reports the chain rather than substituting it"),
  which is a defensible choice — but nothing then offers the final response *as well*.
- The hop requests/responses are sent through `sender.AuthorisedSender.FollowRedirectsAfterPolicy`
  and are never `store.Put`, so they are not in HTTP history either.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Read the response they set the option to get. Configure "Follow redirections: Always", send a login
POST, and the UI shows the 302's body in the response pane plus a badge reading `final 200`. The 200's
bytes — the page that says whether the login worked — exist nowhere: not in the response pane, not in
the hop table, not in HTTP history, not in the message store.

## Note on shape

`Final` is already available at the one call site. Options: return the final response body alongside
`response` (letting the panel offer a first/final toggle), or `store.Put` each hop's request/response
and return their message ids so the hop table rows become clickable. The second is closer to Burp
("the full requests and responses in the redirection chain are stored with each result item") and
would also make the chain visible in history; it needs a decision about whether hop exchanges appear
in HTTP history as `SourceRepeater` rows, since that changes what history counts.
acceptance_criteria: After a followed chain, the operator can read the final response's bytes; the chain's hop requests and responses are reachable, whether returned alongside the first response or stored and linked from the hop table.
notes: Implementation complete in working tree (burpsy-go): sender hops carry their wire bytes (RedirectHop.RequestRaw/ResponseRaw, engine-side, json:"-"), Response.Raw carries the exact bytes a response arrived as, and the web layer maps them onto repeaterHop.request/response for the panel; UI offers First/Final response toggle + per-hop View response buttons. Tests: TestAFollowedHopKeepsTheBytesItSentAndReceived, TestAnUnfollowedHopCarriesNoBytes, TestTheRawEntryKeepsTheFirstResponseBytesOnFinal (sender), TestRepeaterServesTheChainHopsBytesAlongsideTheSend + byteless-refused-hop assertions (web). Java evidence (source of truth /root/burp-re): Burp stores the full redirect-chain requests and responses with each result item (documentation), and Zx9i/Zxrb.Zv render hop authority host:port for non-default ports. Follow-up fix discovered by the new tests: redirectRequest set the hop's Host header to the bare hostname, dropping a non-default port - contradicts Burp's Zxrb.Zv authority rendering (host only for https/443 and http/80, host:port otherwise; :authority rewritten on cross-domain h2 hops) and RFC 9112 3.2; fixed via hostPortFor, which now also brackets IPv6 literals the way Zxrb.Zv does.
close_reason: Fixed. A followed chain now answers the question the option asks in bytes: the engine keeps the wire truth (RedirectHop.RequestRaw/ResponseRaw, Response.Raw on the final response; hop requests rendered once so the scope gate authorises exactly the bytes the transport writes, hops sent via SendAs under the same rules as the operator's own send), the web layer maps them onto repeaterHop.request/response riding the send's own response, and the Repeater pane offers First/Final response plus per-hop 'View response' in the chain table — the chain is additive,  stays the operator's own. Follow-up fix the new tests caught: redirectRequest advertised the hop's Host as the bare hostname, dropping a non-default port — contradicts Burp's decompiled Zxrb.Zv authority rendering (host only for https/443 and http/80, host:port otherwise, IPv6 bracketed; :authority rewritten per hop on h2) and RFC 9112 3.2; hostPortFor now mirrors it. Evidence: sender tests TestAFollowedHopKeepsTheBytesItSentAndReceived / TestAnUnfollowedHopCarriesNoBytes / TestTheRawEntryKeepsTheFirstResponseBytesOnFinal, web test TestRepeaterServesTheChainHopsBytesAlongsideTheSend + byteless-refused-hop assertions; go build/vet/gofmt clean, whole-tree go test 38 pkgs ok, e2e-go.sh 24/0, e2e-ui 157 unit + axe green — e2e-ui's 8 failing specs fail identically at HEAD (bisected in a separate worktree) and are filed separately.

title: intruder: Grep match and Grep extract are regexes but are labelled and placeheld as literal strings, so following the placeholder silently yields nothing
description:
Intruder's Settings tab labels its two grep fields as literal-string controls and gives placeholders
that are literal strings. The server compiles both with `regexp.Compile`. Following either
placeholder produces a control that silently does nothing useful.

## The two controls

`internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:1050-1061`:

    <Field label="Grep match" hint="Counts responses containing this string.">
      ... placeholder="error, root:, welcome"

    <Field label="Grep extract" hint="Captures the text after this marker.">
      ... placeholder="token="

And the section heading, `:1047`: "Count responses containing a marker, or capture a value out of
each response."

## What the server actually does

- `internal/web/api_tools.go:736-752` (`buildGrep`) — `regexp.Compile(*matchRe)` and
  `regexp.Compile(*extractRe)`. Both fields are regular expressions.
- `internal/intruder/engine.go:79-82` — extract returns "the first capture group of the first match,
  or the whole match when the pattern has no groups".

## Consequences, following the UI's own placeholders

1. **Grep match** — typing `error, root:, welcome` (the placeholder) compiles to a regex matching that
   exact 20-character sequence including the commas and spaces. It will never match. The comma-
   separated placeholder also implies Burp's *list* of expressions, which this field is not.
2. **Grep extract** — typing `token=` (the placeholder) compiles to a pattern with no capture group,
   so per `engine.go:79-82` the "extracted" value is the literal string `token=` for every matching
   response. The hint promises "the text after this marker"; the operator gets the marker back. To get
   the value they must know to write `token=([^&\s;]+)` — which nothing in the UI tells them.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html`:

> **Match type** - Specify whether the expressions are simple strings or regular expressions.

Burp makes the distinction an explicit control, precisely because the two behave differently. Burp's
grep-extract is configured through a dialog that defines the location of the item (see
`.../scanner/...response extraction rules`), not a bare pattern.

## Classification

UX DIVERGENCE — a mislabeled control. The plumbing is correct end to end; the label and placeholder
instruct a use that yields wrong results, which is worse than an empty field because the operator has
no reason to doubt it.

## What an operator cannot do

Trust either field. A password-spray attack configured with the suggested `error, root:, welcome`
reports zero grep matches and the operator concludes there were none.

## Fix options (pick one, this needs a decision)

1. **Relabel only** — cheapest. Say "regular expression", change the placeholders to real regexes
   (`error|root:|welcome` and `token=([^&\s;]+)`), and state that extract returns capture group 1 or
   the whole match.
2. **Add Burp's Match type toggle** — simple string vs regex, quoting the literal with
   `regexp.QuoteMeta` when simple. Matches Burp and keeps existing configs working.

(2) is the parity answer; (1) alone stops the misinformation and should land regardless. Burp's other
grep options — case sensitivity, exclude HTTP headers, expression *list* — are filed separately.
acceptance_criteria: The two grep fields either state that they take a regular expression with placeholders that work as written, or gain Burp's simple-string/regex Match type toggle; typing the placeholder value produces the behaviour the label promises.
close_reason:
Done in 0fe8857. Both fix options from the issue, one per field, and no engine change.

Grep match — option 2, Burp's Match type toggle. A new 'Match type' select offers Simple string / Regular expression. In simple mode the literal is quoted before it is sent, with `quoteRegex` escaping exactly the byte set `regexp.QuoteMeta` escapes (`\\.+*?()|[]{}^$`) — pinned by test, including that a quoted literal with metacharacters matches itself and not a regex interpretation of itself. Placeholders now work as written in both modes: `root:` in simple, `error|root:|welcome` in regex. The hint states which is which.

Grep extract — option 1, relabel. Now 'Grep extract (regular expression)', hint 'Captures the first capture group of the first match, or the whole match when the pattern has no group. A pattern with no group returns the marker itself.' Placeholder is `token=([^&\s;]+)`, which produces the value the old hint falsely promised. The section heading changed from 'Count responses containing a marker' to 'Count the responses that match'.

Existing configurations keep working: regex mode sends the pattern unchanged, and simple mode is the new default only for a field that starts empty.

NOT done: Burp's other grep options — case sensitivity, exclude HTTP headers, and the expression *list* — which the issue says are filed separately. Extract is still a bare pattern rather than Burp's start/end-delimiter dialog.

title: intruder: navigating to another page destroys the whole attack configuration and the finished report
description:
All Intruder state lives in component-local `useState`. Only the active page is mounted, so clicking
any other nav entry unmounts the page and destroys the message id, the discovered positions, the
selection, all seven payload-source forms, the processing rules, the grep settings, the limits, and
the finished attack report. Coming back shows an empty Intruder.

This is not a reload-persistence gap — it happens on ordinary in-app navigation, and Repeater in the
same app does not behave this way.

## Burp-side evidence

Burp opens each attack in its own window (`/root/burp-re/BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md:176`,
`intruderAttackFrameResultItemTabBar`), so switching to Repeater cannot affect it, and
`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html`
→ **Save attack** writes an attack to the project file. `.../results/saving-attacks.html` and
`.../configure-attack/managing-tabs.html` cover the same ground: an Intruder attack is a durable
object in Burp, not a transient form.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:338-361` — 22 `useState` hooks hold everything:
  `msgId`, `target`, `label`, `mode`, `allPoints`, `points`, `selected`, `payloadTexts`,
  `payloadTypes`, `payloadNumbers`, `payloadFiles`, `payloadBrute`, `payloadDates`, `payloadCustom`,
  `payloadNulls`, `rules`, `grepMatch`, `grepExtract`, `maxRequests`, `maxInFlight`, `rps`, `result`.
- `internal/web/ui/src/lib/store.ts` — the only Intruder key in the shared store is `intruderSeed`
  (`:110`, `:166`, `:311`), which is the one-shot send-to handoff and is cleared on arrival
  (`pages/intruder.tsx:376`).
- `internal/web/ui/src/lib/store.ts:321-335` — `partialize` persists `repeaterTabs`,
  `activeRepeaterTab` and `repeaterGroups`. Nothing from Intruder appears.
- `internal/web/ui/src/app.tsx:162` and `:664` — `const ActivePage = leaf.page;` … `<ActivePage />`.
  One page is mounted at a time, so a route change unmounts Intruder and React discards its state.

Verified this is Intruder-specific: Repeater drafts survive both navigation and reload because they
are in the store (`pages/repeater.tsx:29-33` reads tabs from `useApp`).

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Leave the page. A completed 5,000-request attack report is destroyed by clicking "Repeater" to check a
header value, along with the payload sets and processing rules that produced it. There is no warning
and no way back — the attack cannot be re-run either, because the configuration went with it.

## Suggested shape

Minimum: move the Intruder configuration into the zustand store and add it to `partialize`, the way
Repeater tabs already are. Better, and closer to Burp: make a launched attack a named object with its
report, so several attacks coexist and a report outlives the form that produced it. The second option
needs a decision on where reports live (client store vs. a server-side attack registry) — a
server-side registry would also give the stop/pause work filed separately something to address.
acceptance_criteria: Leaving Intruder and returning preserves the base request, positions, payload sets, processing rules, grep settings, limits and the last attack report.
close_reason:
Done in 0fe8857 (option 1 from the issue: the configuration moved into the zustand store and into partialize, the way Repeater tabs already are — plus the report).

- `IntruderConfig` in lib/store.ts holds all 22 former useState fields (msgId, target, label, mode, allPoints, points, selected, the seven payload forms, rules, grep, limits) plus the two new ones this wave added (grepMatchMode, poolName).
- `IntruderRun` holds the finished report, the legacy shape, and a payload snapshot taken at launch. `intruderTab` remembers the open sub-tab.
- All three are in partialize, so they survive reload as well as navigation. The report is bounded by the server's detail_limit (500 attempt rows), so this is tens of kilobytes.
- partialize became a named export `persistedWorkspace` so the rule is assertable: zustand's persist API is not attached when there is no localStorage, which is every bun test run.
- The page keeps its old shape: a `field(key)` helper returns a useState-style setter per field, so the JSX and the payload-set length sync are unchanged.

Two things the fix had to get right beyond 'it persists':
- A send-to handoff from History/Repeater now replaces only what is tied to the specific request (msgId, target, label, points, selected) and clears the report. Payload sets, rules, grep and limits are the operator's typed work and a send-to is not consent to discard it.
- Persistence with no way out is its own trap, so the header gained 'New attack', which is the deliberate full reset and asks for confirmation first.

Tests: src/lib/intruder-state.test.ts — the store holds and patches the config, holds the report, remembers the tab; persistedWorkspace carries intruder/intruderRun/intruderTab and still excludes intruderSeed and closedRepeaterTabs.

NOT done, and deliberately: the 'better, closer to Burp' option — several named attacks coexisting with a server-side registry. That needs the decision the issue names on where reports live, and it is the thing wub (pause/resume/stop) would build on.

title: intruder: each attempt's stored response id is returned to the browser and no UI code reads it, so result responses are unreachable
description:
Every Intruder attempt's response is stored in the message store and its id is returned to the
browser, but no UI code reads that id. The response bytes behind an interesting result are
unreachable.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/results/viewing-results.html`
— selecting a row in the results table shows that item's full request and response in the panes
below. The `Store requests / responses` setting in
`.../configure-attack/settings.html` exists precisely so this is possible, and its stated benefits
are "View requests and responses in full during an attack / Repeat individual requests if necessary /
Send requests or responses to other Burp tools".

## burpsy-side evidence

The id is produced, plumbed and then dropped:

- `internal/web/api_tools.go:640-643` — `record` puts every response into the store and returns the
  id:

      record := func(raw []byte) uint64 {
          id, _ := s.store.Put(raw, core.DirectionResponse)
          return uint64(id)
      }

- `internal/intruder/engine.go:225` — `Attempt.ResponseID *uint64` with tag `json:"response_id"`, so
  it is serialised to the browser on every attempt.
- `internal/web/ui/src/lib/types.tools.ts:102` — `response_id: number | null` is declared in the TS
  view type, and `:85` declares `example_response_id: number | null` for buckets.
- Nothing consumes either:

      $ grep -rn "response_id" internal/web/ui/src/
      internal/web/ui/src/lib/types.tools.ts:85:  example_response_id: number | null;
      internal/web/ui/src/lib/types.tools.ts:102:  response_id: number | null;

  Two hits, both the type declaration itself, zero consumers. Positive control on the same file:
  `grep -rn "grep_extract" internal/web/ui/src/lib/types.tools.ts` → 2 hits at `:87` and `:105`, and
  those *are* consumed at `pages/intruder.tsx:225,323`.
- The retrieval path exists and is used elsewhere: `useMessage` in
  `internal/web/ui/src/lib/data.ts` already fetches a stored message by id, and Intruder itself calls
  it for the base request (`pages/intruder.tsx:365, 706-718`).

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP. This is the closest thing to a decorative control I found in Intruder, but it is not
one: the value is genuinely produced and acted on by the server (the response really is stored) —
it is the *frontend* that ignores a field the backend went to the trouble of returning.

## What an operator cannot do

Look at the response that made a result interesting. A row shows `200 / 4.1 kB / reflected` and the
bytes behind it are in the store, addressable, and unreachable from the screen showing the row.

## Acceptance note

Both `response_id` (attempts) and `example_response_id` (buckets) should become clickable; the bucket
one matters most because buckets are the default view and the only one that names a payload today.
acceptance_criteria: An operator can open the stored request/response for any attempt row and any result bucket from the Results tab; response_id and example_response_id have consumers in pages/, not only declarations in types.tools.ts.
close_reason:
Done in 0fe8857 (UI only; no Go change needed — the ids were already on the wire).

Both fields now have consumers in pages/intruder.tsx, not just declarations in types.tools.ts:
- attempts table gained a Response column reading `attempt.response_id`;
- result buckets gained one reading `bucket.example_response_id`.

Each renders a ResponseCell: a View button that opens the stored bytes in a Modal via the existing `useMessage` hook (the same path Intruder already used for the base request), with loading, error and no-bytes-stored distinguished in the editor body. A null id renders a dim em dash titled 'No response was stored for this attempt' rather than a dead button.

Evidence: `grep -rn 'response_id' src/` now hits pages/intruder.tsx as well as the type declarations. tsc --noEmit clean; test:lib 131 pass (was 99).

title: intruder: the Results attempts table shows an ordinal but never the payload that produced the row
description:
The Attempts table in Intruder's Results tab shows an ordinal and no payload. There is no column, no
tooltip and no expansion that says which payload produced a given row.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/results/viewing-results.html`
— the results table's columns are item #, **Payload**, status, error, timeout, length, plus one column
per configured grep expression. The spec at `/root/burp-re/BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md:176`
records "Result table showing Payload, Status, Length, Error, Time". Payload is the second column and
the reason the table exists.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:307` — the headers are literally:

      <SimpleTable headers={["#", "Status", "Length", "Time", "Reflected", "Grep", "Error"]}>

- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:308-326` — each row renders `attempt.ordinal` and nothing
  that names a payload.
- The payload *is* recoverable. `internal/web/api_tools.go:754-770` (`payloadsAt`) reconstructs the
  exact combination behind any ordinal from the plan — its own doc comment says "This is why results
  can hold an ordinal and nothing else: the plan is a pure function of the index." But the handler
  only calls it for bucket first-ordinals (`internal/web/api_tools.go:667-672`), so
  `RunView.Examples` covers buckets and not attempts.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:458-461` — the UI's `examples` map is keyed on
  `first_ordinal`, so even client-side there is nothing to join an attempt row against.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Read the results table. Attempt #4173 returned 200 with an interesting length, and there is no way to
learn which payload caused it — the operator would have to re-derive the plan's ordinal arithmetic by
hand (for a cluster bomb, a mixed-radix decode across N sets).

## Note on the cheap fix

The server already has `payloadsAt(plan, resolved, ordinal)`. Extending `AttemptView`/`Attempt` with
the resolved payload list, or extending `RunView.Examples` to cover every returned attempt ordinal
(bounded by `report.detail_limit`, `internal/intruder/engine.go:247`), plus a Payload column, is the
whole change. Note `Attempts` is already capped server-side, so this does not unbound the response.
acceptance_criteria: Each attempt row displays the payload combination behind it, resolved via payloadsAt, for every attempt the server returns.
close_reason: Payload column already existed client-side from an earlier commit, but rows past a bucket's first ordinal showed pre-payload-processing-rule text (stale for add_prefix/hash/etc). Fixed server-side: internal/web/api_tools.go now adds an examples entry for every attempt ordinal (not just bucket first-ordinals), resolved via payloadsAt against the post-rule 'resolved' sets, bounded by report.DetailLimit. New regression test TestIntruderRunExamplesCoverEveryAttemptWithThePostRulePayload in internal/web/intruder_api_test.go. go build/vet/test and tsc --noEmit all pass. Uncommitted per conservative git profile.

comments.author: FixIntruderUI
comments.text:
Substantially fixed in 0fe8857 but NOT closed — the payload *text* is not recoverable in the browser for generator-backed sets, and that needs the Go change this agent was told not to make.

## What landed

The attempts table has a Payload column as its second column, and every row resolves.

The ordinal decode is a faithful port of `(*AttackPlan).Fill` (internal/intruder/plan.go:240), in lib/types.tools.ts:
- `planSetLengths` mirrors NewAttackPlan's `setsUsed` (single-set modes read set 0; multi-set modes read one set per position, truncated to the sets that exist);
- `assignmentAt` mirrors Fill for all four modes, including cluster bomb's mixed-radix decode with set 0 as the *fastest*-varying digit;
- set lengths come from the report's own `payload_sets[].count`, so the arithmetic runs against the sets the engine used rather than the sets the form currently holds;
- `report.planned` bounds valid ordinals, so an out-of-plan ordinal returns no answer instead of a wrong one.

Where a bucket's first ordinal is involved the server's own `examples` entry is used directly, so those rows are the server's answer, not a recomputation — which also cross-checks the port at runtime.

Payload text is resolved against a snapshot of the payload sets taken at the moment of launch (stored beside the report), not read live: editing the forms after a run must not relabel the rows of a report those forms did not produce.

## The remaining gap, precisely

The browser can only name the payloads of a set it is itself the source of truth for: a Simple list, and null payloads. `intruder.PayloadSet.Items` is tagged `json:"-"` (internal/intruder/payload.go:98), so the resolved items of a file, numbers, brute-force, dates or custom-iterator set never cross the wire. For those, a row shows the position — 'set 2 payload #18' — dimmed, with a tooltip explaining why. It says which payload, not what it is.

A set whose server-reported `count` disagrees with the browser's list is also treated as unnameable, which is what a payload processing rule that skipped an item looks like from here: the skip shifts every index after it, so the browser's list is not the list the ordinals were computed against. That check is deliberate and self-verifying — without it, rules would have produced confidently wrong payload text.

So: for the default configuration (Simple list, no processing rules) the column shows real payloads for every row and the issue is done. For a wordlist or a generator, or with any processing rule configured, it shows positions.

## What would close it

The cheap fix the issue already describes, on the server: extend `RunView.Examples` to cover every returned attempt ordinal (bounded by `report.detail_limit` = 500, so the response stays bounded), or add the resolved payloads to `Attempt`. `payloadsAt(plan, resolved, ordinal)` already exists and `resolved` is post-rule, so it is correct where the browser cannot be. About a dozen lines in internal/web/api_tools.go around :664. The UI needs no further change: it already prefers a server-supplied example over its own decode for any ordinal, so extending Examples makes every row exact automatically.

Evidence: tsc --noEmit clean; test:lib 131 pass (was 99), 32 new in src/lib/types.tools.test.ts and src/lib/intruder-state.test.ts. The plan-port expectations are derived from plan.go rather than from the port's output — cluster bomb's spray ordering is pinned by test because decoding it backwards would label every row confidently wrong.

comments.author: FixBackendTruth
comments.text:
PREMISE VERIFIED AT HEAD (8654a1b) by FixBackendTruth. NOT STARTED — pulled off implementation by the operator's change of direction. Recording the verification so the inventory does not have to re-derive it.

Every load-bearing fact in the proposed server-side fix holds at HEAD:

1. internal/intruder/payload.go:98 — 'Items []string `json:"-"`'. Confirmed. The resolved, post-rule payload items genuinely never cross the wire, so FixIntruderUI's read is correct and its browser-side decode really is the best the client can do. Also confirmed on the same struct: Count (:100) IS serialised, which is what makes the client's count-disagreement heuristic possible — a payload processing rule that skipped an item shows up as a count mismatch, and since a skip shifts every later index, treating that set as unnameable is the right refusal rather than a confident wrong label.

2. payloadsAt(plan, resolved, ordinal) exists at internal/web/api_tools.go:850 and is a pure function of the ordinal — the plan derives request i from i. Confirmed.

3. 'resolved' at the Examples build site IS post-rule: chain.Run(ps) is applied during resolution, before the plan is built, which is why plan.Len() is the request count and a rule-dropped payload never occupies an ordinal. So the server can be exact exactly where the browser cannot. Confirmed.

4. The Examples loop is at api_tools.go:758-759, currently 'for _, b := range report.Buckets' taking only each bucket's FirstOrdinal. Extending it to every returned attempt ordinal is the right shape.

5. The detail_limit bound is real: Attack.DetailLimit defaults to 500 (internal/intruder/engine.go, NewAttack) and report.Attempts is already capped by it, so iterating report.Attempts rather than the plan keeps the response bounded by a limit that already exists. This is what makes the fix safe.

SCOPE ESTIMATE: small. Roughly 10 lines at api_tools.go:758 plus a test. Comparable to burpsy-react-ui-2v5, not to eip or wub.

TWO THINGS THE PROPOSED FIX MUST STATE OUT LOUD, both of which are real remaining limits rather than defects:

(a) BEYOND detail_limit (500) there are no examples and rows still show positions. On any attack over 500 requests the Results table is exact for the first 500 and positional after. That must be visible in the UI, not discovered by an operator on a large attack. Note the interaction: report.Attempts is capped at 500 but BUCKETS are not, and a bucket's FirstOrdinal can exceed 500 — so the current per-bucket Examples can name a payload for an ordinal that has no attempt row. Extending Examples to attempt ordinals must ADD to the bucket examples, not replace them, or large attacks would lose naming they have today.

(b) The legacy flat-array response shape (req.Mode/PayloadSets/PayloadSources all nil) carries AttemptView with its own 'payload' field and no Examples at all. It is a different projection and this fix does not touch it. Worth confirming which shape intruder.tsx actually posts before anyone claims the table is fixed.

ONE THING TO VERIFY RATHER THAN TRUST, per the task as written: that intruder.tsx really does prefer a server-supplied example over its own decode for any ordinal. I did not check this — it is in a file I do not own. If the preference is client-first, or keyed only to bucket ordinals, extending Examples changes nothing and the issue is not closeable on the server change alone.

title: intruder: a running attack cannot be paused, resumed or stopped, and its dashboard task is not registered as cancellable
description:
A launched Intruder attack runs to completion. There is no pause, no resume, no stop in the UI, no
API route that could stop one, and the dashboard task the attack registers is not cancellable either.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html`
— the attack results window has a manual pause/resume control ("You can resume the attack at any time
by clicking"), and `results/workflow.html` covers stopping an attack. The spec at
`/root/burp-re/BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md:176` records the per-attack results window.

## burpsy-side evidence

- Only two Intruder routes exist: `internal/web/server.go:742-743` —
  `/api/intruder/points` and `/api/intruder/run`. There is no stop/pause route to call.
- `internal/web/ui/src/lib/data.tools.ts:101-105` — `useIntruderRun` is a bare `useMutation` with no
  `AbortController`. Compare `useRepeaterSend` in the same file, `:89-91`, which does have one
  (`cancel: () => inFlight.current?.abort()`), so the pattern exists and was not applied here.
- `internal/web/api_tools.go:634` — the dashboard task is registered with
  `s.tasks.Start(dash.KindIntruder, ...)` and **never** calls `Handle.WithCancel`. Therefore
  `Task.Cancellable()` (`internal/dash/tasks.go:140`) is false for every attack and the dashboard
  renders no stop button for it.
- Contrast, same tree: `internal/web/api_sequencer_capture.go:448` and
  `internal/web/api_discovery.go:400` both do `ctx, cancel := task.WithCancel(...)`, which is what
  makes those tasks stoppable from the dashboard.
- `internal/web/api_tools.go:637` — `report := intruder.Run(attack, send, record)` is a synchronous
  call inside the HTTP handler, so there is no handle to a running attack at all.

A pause/stop engine *does* exist but is not on this path: `internal/intruder/intruder.go:336`
(`Stop()`), `:302` (`setProgressStatus`) and `:57` (`Status string // "running", "paused",
"completed", "stopped"`). Its only non-test caller is the CLI —
`grep -rn "NewIntruder" --include=*.go . | grep -v _test.go` → `cmd/burpsy/cli.go:163` only.

Absence grep for the auto-pause feature specifically:

    $ grep -rli "auto_pause|autopause" internal/intruder internal/web/api_tools.go internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx
    (no output)

Positive control, same paths in the same invocation: `grep -rli "baseline" ...` →
`internal/intruder/engine_test.go`.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Stop an attack. A cluster bomb bounded at the 200,000-request ceiling
(`intruderMaxBound`, `internal/web/api_tools.go:281`) aimed at the wrong host cannot be halted from
Intruder or from the Dashboard; the only recourse is killing the browser's request or the server.

## Note

Burp's `Auto-pause attack` (pause when an expression appears in or is missing from a response) is a
separate control and is filed separately; it is blocked on this one, because there is nothing to
pause.
acceptance_criteria: An in-flight attack can be stopped from the Intruder screen and from the Dashboard task row, the attack's dash.Handle registers WithCancel, and stopping produces a report marked as stopped rather than an error.
close_reason: Fixed in 6427834. The audit was right that internal/dash already had the primitive - dash.Handle.WithCancel's own doc names 'intruder attack stop' as one of its three consumers, and this handler never called it. It does now, so Task.Cancellable() is true and the dashboard stop button works today. But WithCancel alone was NOT enough, which the audit did not anticipate: cancelling the send context leaves the driver loop enumerating the plan, so an attack halted at request 12 of 200,000 reports 199,988 failures for requests the target never received. So internal/intruder/control.go adds a real Control - the driver loop gates before each plan position, pause blocks on a condition variable, Stop broadcasts so a paused attack is stoppable, and in-flight sends at a pause are collected because the target already received them. AttackReport gains status/stop_reason/enumerated: Planned/Sent cannot distinguish 'the operator stopped it' from 'the target refused them', and the dash task now gets Stop() rather than Finish() so Task.Complete() refuses to call a prefix of the payload set a complete answer. Routes: GET /api/intruder/attacks, POST /api/intruder/attacks/{task_id}/{pause|resume|stop}, keyed by dashboard task id so both stop buttons address the same attack by the same name; 404 (no such attack) and 409 (past acting on) kept apart. /run stays synchronous - making it a background job changes its contract and every client of it - so a paused attack holds its own response open, which is honest: the report does not exist yet. Mutation: removing the driver gate fails TestStopHaltsTheDriverLoopRatherThanFailingEveryRemainingOrdinal ('1000 requests were sent after a stop at the third'), TestPauseHoldsTheAttackAndResumeReleasesIt and TestStopOnContextReachesTheDriver; swapping task.WithCancel for context.WithCancel fails TestARunningAttackIsCancellableFromTheDashboard. UI HALF OPEN and listed in uiRouteMissingSurface against this issue (NOT uiRouteExempt - nothing justifies the absence): intruder.tsx needs an AbortController on its run mutation (useRepeaterSend in the same module has one) and controls wired to the two routes.

comments.author: FixBackendTruth
comments.text:
SCOPE NOTE for the inventory (issue is closed/done, this is calibration).

About 3x the filed scope. The audit's guidance — 'internal/dash's Handle already has WithCancel and the registry has a cancellable concept, check what exists before building' — was right and I did reuse both, but it led to an estimate that was too small for a reason worth recording.

WithCancel ALONE DOES NOT STOP AN ATTACK. It stops the sends. The driver loop in intruder.Run keeps enumerating the plan, and every remaining ordinal becomes a send error against a cancelled context. An attack halted at request 12 of 200,000 would have reported 12 sent and 199,988 failed across up to 2,000 error buckets — a report claiming the target refused 199,988 requests it never received. That is a worse defect than the missing button, and it is the shape any 'make X cancellable by wiring WithCancel' issue in this tree should be checked for: cancellation only works where the work polls it, and a loop that hands each iteration to a context-aware callee is NOT polling it.

So the real fix was three parts, not one:
1. internal/intruder/control.go — a Control the driver loop gates on before each plan position. Pause blocks on a condition variable; Stop broadcasts so a paused attack is stoppable rather than parked forever.
2. AttackReport gains status/stop_reason/enumerated. Planned/Sent cannot express 'stopped': 12-of-200,000 is either the operator's button or a finding about the target, and those were indistinguishable. The dash task also needed Stop() rather than Finish() so Task.Complete() refuses to call a prefix of the payload set a complete answer.
3. The routes and the registry.

DESIGN CONSTRAINT the issue did not mention, and the main reason the UI half is still open: api_tools.go:637's 'report := intruder.Run(...)' is synchronous inside the HTTP handler, and the audit noted this ('there is no handle to a running attack at all'). I did NOT change that. Making /run a background job changes its response contract and every client of it, which is a UI change and outside my lane. The consequence a future engineer must know: a paused attack holds its own /run request open, because the report genuinely does not exist yet. The controls work from another connection, which is why the routes are keyed by dashboard task id.

REMAINING (UI, sized): intruder.tsx needs (a) an AbortController on its run mutation — useRepeaterSend in lib/data.tools.ts:89-91 has the pattern — and (b) buttons hitting POST /api/intruder/attacks/{task_id}/{pause|resume|stop}. The awkward part is learning task_id while the run is in flight: the /run response only arrives at the end, so the page must poll GET /api/intruder/attacks. Both routes are listed in uiRouteMissingSurface against this issue, and that list self-cleans — TestNoKnownGapWasQuietlyFixed fails until the entries are deleted once a caller exists. The dashboard stop button works today with no UI work at all.

comments.author: FixBackendTruth
comments.text:
LIVE INACCURACY INTRODUCED BY THE GO HALF (6427834). Raised by FixIntruderUI, verified by me at HEAD. This is not a future risk — it is true now.

internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:324 renders 'of {formatCount(report.planned)} planned'. The dashboard stop button works TODAY with no UI work, because 6427834 made the task cancellable. So: cancel an intruder task from the Dashboard, and the Results panel reads 'Sent 12 of 400 planned' — which states that the target was asked 400 times and answered 12. It was asked 12 times. The other 388 plan positions were never enumerated.

That is the same class of defect as the five I was sent to fix: the UI making a false statement about what happened. I introduced the reachable stop that exposes it. The Go side reports the correct denominator (report.enumerated, plus status and stop_reason) — the panel does not read it yet.

FIX, small and located: intruder.tsx:324 should use report.enumerated as the denominator when report.status is 'stopped', and the caveats array at :306 — which already exists to say what was bounded away — should carry report.stop_reason. FixIntruderUI's judgement that this must land in the SAME change as any stop control is right, and I would go further: it should land BEFORE or WITH the controls, because the falsehood is already reachable via the Dashboard.

PRIORITY NOTE for the inventory: if the UI half of this issue is deferred, this one line is worth splitting out and doing on its own. Everything else here is a missing capability, which is visible. This is a wrong number, which is not.

OWNERSHIP: intruder.tsx is not mine and I have not touched it. Not fixed by me, and I am under a stop-implementing instruction.

Four further constraints from FixIntruderUI (commit 0fe8857, all in intruder.tsx an hour ago), recorded here so the inventory reads from the tracker:

1. Aborting the run's fetch stops the browser waiting but does NOT stop the attack — only POST /api/intruder/attacks/{id}/stop does. So Cancel must call the stop route and only then abort, or it is the dishonest Cancel that useRepeaterSend's doc comment warns about. Read that comment before copying the mechanism.

2. Learning task_id mid-flight via GET /api/intruder/attacks needs a matching key, and target+kind+planned is NOT unique — two identical sniper attacks on one host are indistinguishable, so list-and-guess can stop the wrong attack. FixIntruderUI proposes returning the id early instead (a first SSE frame, or a 202 carrying the id before the run body). I agree that is the better contract; it is a change to /run's response shape, which is why I did not make it unilaterally. Whoever takes this should decide it first, because it changes the UI design.

3. Intruder state now lives in the zustand store (lib/store.ts, IntruderConfig / IntruderRun), not component useState. A live attack's task_id belongs there but must NOT be persisted to persistedWorkspace: a stale id after a restart addresses an attack that no longer exists, or one that has since taken the id. My registry is in-process and empty after a restart, so a persisted id would 404 at best and mis-target at worst.

4. uiRouteMissingSurface is untouched; I re-ran TestNoKnownGapWasQuietlyFixed and TestEveryOperatorFacingRouteIsReferencedFromTheConsole at HEAD and both pass, so the two entries are still accurate. Routes are at internal/web/server.go:752-753.

comments.author: FixIntruderUI
comments.text:
The wrong-number half of this issue is fixed in 09acaf8 (UI only). The missing capability — pause/resume/stop controls — is untouched and this issue stays open for it.

FixBackendTruth was right that it was live, not future, and I confirmed it at HEAD before touching anything: api_tools.go:711 registers a cancel against the dashboard task, and dashboard.tsx:121-129 already offers Cancel on any cancellable running task. So cancelling an intruder attack from the Dashboard produced a report reading 'Sent 12 of 400 planned' — asserting the target was asked 400 times and answered 12, when it was asked 12.

What landed:
- `attackProgress(report)` in lib/types.tools.ts derives {stopped, paused, reached} in one place. `reached` is `report.enumerated`, the plan positions actually driven.
- The Sent metric reads 'of N reached · plan was M' when stopped, and the card is flagged.
- The caveats list gains a first entry naming the stop, its stop_reason, and stating that everything below describes a prefix of the payload sets rather than the whole attack.

The part worth reviewing: `status` and `enumerated` are declared optional in the TS types because an older server sends neither, and absent is read as completed over `planned`. That is sound ONLY because no server that omits those fields could stop an attack, so completed is what it always was. It is written down in attackProgress's doc comment because a future field that changes that must not reuse the absence. Also `?? planned` rather than `|| planned`: an enumerated of 0 is a real count and 400 would be a fabrication. Six tests pin both.

Still open on this issue, unchanged:
- the pause/resume/stop controls in intruder.tsx against POST /api/intruder/attacks/{task_id}/{action};
- the two decisions FixBackendTruth recorded — whether /run returns the task_id early (target+kind+planned is not a unique key, so list-and-guess can stop the wrong attack) and the Cancel-must-stop-before-abort ordering;
- deleting the two uiRouteMissingSurface entries when the routes gain callers. I did not touch that list, so it is still accurate.

Also unchanged: report.session_cookies has no consumer. That belongs to 39m, and it is a missing display rather than a wrong number, so it is visible in a way this was not.

title: intruder: insertion-point discovery ignores JSON, XML and base64 bodies, so a JSON API request yields one whole-body position
description:
Intruder's insertion-point discoverer only parses `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` bodies. A JSON,
XML or multipart body yields exactly one insertion point — the whole body — so no individual field
can be attacked.

The same product already has a body parser that does this properly; it is just not the one wired to
Intruder.

## Burp-side evidence

Burp discovers JSON and XML parameters as individual insertion points and escapes payloads for the
container. Its own documentation names the families under
`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/positions.html`,
and the request-parameter model is exercised throughout
`.../testing-workflow/analyzing/evaluating-inputs.html`.

## burpsy-side evidence

The weak parser Intruder uses:

- `internal/intruder/points.go:198-207` — body key/value points are pushed **only** when
  Content-Type contains `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`:

      isForm := false
      if ct := msg.Header("content-type"); ... bytes.Contains(bytes.ToLower(ct), []byte("application/x-www-form-urlencoded")) {
          isForm = true
      }
      if isForm && (cfg.BodyParams || cfg.ParamNames) { pushKVPoints(...) }

- `internal/intruder/points.go:209-215` — everything else falls through to a single
  `PointEntireBody` labelled `"body"`.
- `internal/intruder/points.go:222-236` (`pushKVPoints`) splits on `&` and `=` only.

The strong parser, already in the tree and used by the Scanner:

- `internal/bcheck/insertion.go:645-646` — discovers every JSON string value in a body.
- `internal/bcheck/insertion.go:1012-1106` (`jsonStringValues`) — key-aware JSON walk.
- `internal/bcheck/insertion.go:795, 1140-1141` (`jsonEscape`) — escapes the payload so the body
  stays well-formed.
- `internal/bcheck/insertion.go:201-212` — `nestedKind` covers `json`, `base64→json`, `base64`, `xml`.
- `internal/bcheck/insertion.go:1335` — nested points inside a base64-wrapped JSON value.
- `internal/bcheck/insertion.go:229-240` — `Declined` explicitly records multipart / non-UTF-8 bodies
  as refused rather than silently empty.

Confirmed by test names at HEAD: `internal/bcheck/insertion_test.go:62`
(`TestJSONStringValuesArePointsAndNumbersAreNot`) and `:150`
(`TestAJSONPayloadIsEscapedSoTheBodyStaysWellFormed`).

Absence grep, Intruder side:

    $ grep -rni "json" internal/intruder/points.go
    (no output)

Positive control, same file: `grep -c "func" internal/intruder/points.go` → non-zero, and
`grep -n "PointBodyParamValue" internal/intruder/points.go` → 3 hits.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP — and specifically an internal asymmetry: burpsy has two independent insertion-point
engines and the weaker one is wired to Intruder.

## What an operator cannot do

Fuzz one field of a JSON API request. `POST /login {"user":"bo","pass":"x"}` offers a single "body"
position, so the only attack available replaces the entire JSON document with each payload — which
the server rejects as malformed before the code under test is reached. Modern targets are mostly
JSON, so this removes Intruder from most engagements.

## Decision needed before code

Two options, and they are not equivalent:

1. **Extend `internal/intruder/points.go`** to parse JSON/XML with its own walker. Duplicates logic
   that already exists and will drift from the Scanner's.
2. **Have Intruder consume `internal/bcheck`'s enumerator** and map its points onto
   `intruder.InsertionPoint`. One parser, one escaping policy, and the Scanner's `Declined` reporting
   comes along. Needs an adapter because the two types differ (`bcheck` points carry `BaseValue` and
   per-kind escaping; `intruder.InsertionPoint` carries a `core.Span`).

Recommendation is (2). Whoever picks it up should also decide whether payload escaping is automatic
per container or an opt-in payload-processing rule, because splicing an unescaped `"` into a JSON
string silently changes what is being tested.
acceptance_criteria: A JSON request body produces one insertion point per JSON string value, with container-correct payload escaping, and XML/base64-nested bodies are either supported or explicitly reported as declined.

title: intruder: Positions has no manual payload markers — Burp's Add §/Clear §/Auto § do not exist, positions are auto-discovered only
description:
Intruder's Positions tab offers no way to mark a payload position by hand. Positions are whatever
the discoverer found, and nothing else.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/positions.html`
(Burp's own shipped documentation, 2026.7.1). The Positions tab is a request editor with three
buttons — **Add §**, **Clear §**, **Auto §**. The operator selects any bytes in the template request
and marks them. `Auto §` is the automatic guess; it is the *fallback*, not the only mode. The spec at
`/root/burp-re/BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md:167-168` records the same three buttons.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `internal/intruder/points.go:23-33` — nine fixed `PointKind` families. There is no "manual" or
  "marker" kind, and `InsertionPoint` is only ever constructed by `FindPoints`.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:706-708` — the base-request editor is `readOnly`, so the
  operator cannot even type a marker.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:660-691` — the entire position UI is a checkbox per
  discovered point.
- `internal/web/api_tools.go:344-357` (`selectPoints`) and `intruderRunReq.Points` — the wire
  contract carries *indices into the discovered list*, so a hand-marked span cannot be expressed
  even by an API caller.

Absence grep over both the engine and the page:

    $ grep -rni "marker|§" internal/intruder/points.go internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx
    internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:1047: ... "Count responses containing a marker ..."
    internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:1060: ... hint="Captures the text after this marker."

Both hits are the *grep-extract* help text, unrelated to positions. Positive control on the same two
files: `grep -n "PointKind" internal/intruder/points.go` → 4 hits;
`grep -c "payload" internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx` → 66.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Attack any position the discoverer does not model: a substring of a value (`id=12§34§`), one segment
of a JWT, a field inside a base64 blob, one member of a JSON body, or a slice of a custom binary
parameter. This is the first action in every Burp Intruder workflow.

## Note on scope

The splice path already accepts arbitrary spans — `InsertionPoint{Kind, Span, Label}` plus
`fixContentLength` after every splice (`internal/intruder/points.go:303, 318-327`) will splice a
hand-marked region unchanged. The work is a marker-aware request editor plus a wire shape that can
carry explicit spans alongside discovered indices. Fixing this also subsumes the JSON-body gap filed
separately, because a `§`-capable editor lets an operator target a JSON field by hand.
acceptance_criteria: The Positions tab lets an operator mark an arbitrary byte range in the base request as a payload position, and an attack runs against hand-marked positions as well as discovered ones.

title: intruder: attack requests never carry cookie-jar cookies, so authenticated endpoints cannot be fuzzed
description:
## Claim
Cookie-jar cookies are attached only on the Repeater send path; an Intruder attack against an authenticated endpoint goes out with no session cookie.

## Burp-side evidence
`settings/sessions/session-handling-rules.html` — "Add cookies from the session handling cookie jar" is a rule action, and the Scope tab's **Tools scope** decides which tools it applies to:
> "The Tools scope settings […] enable you to specify the Burp tools that each rule should apply to."

`settings/sessions/index.html` states the jar "is shared between all of Burp's tools", and describes Intruder explicitly receiving session updates:
> "When the Scanner or Intruder makes a request that manipulates a cookie or parameter that is affected by a session handling action, the session handling action is not applied to that request. […] the sessid cookie is updated when Intruder is fuzzing other parameters."

So Burp's behaviour is: Intruder *does* get jar cookies, except on the exact parameter being fuzzed.

## burpsy-side evidence
`s.cookieHeaderFor` is defined at `internal/web/api_tools.go:257` and has exactly one call site:
```
$ grep -rn "cookieHeaderFor" --include=*.go internal/web/ | grep -v _test
internal/web/api_tools.go:120:  rawRequest := opts.applyToRequest([]byte(req.Request), s.cookieHeaderFor(host, port, tls))
internal/web/api_tools.go:254:// cookieHeaderFor returns the session coordinator's cookie header for the target...
internal/web/api_tools.go:257:func (s *Server) cookieHeaderFor(host string, port uint16, tls bool) string {
```
Line 120 is inside the Repeater send handler (the surrounding block validates `req.Options` as `repeaterSendOptions`, `api_tools.go:109-116`).

The intruder engine has no session or jar reference. Per-file counts over `internal/intruder/*.go` (non-test), with `func ` as the positive control:

| file | funcs | /cookie/i | /session/i |
|---|---|---|---|
| breakdown.go | 2 | 0 | 0 |
| engine.go | 15 | 0 | 0 |
| intruder.go | 12 | 0 | 1 |
| limit.go | 17 | 0 | 0 |
| payload.go | 23 | 0 | 0 |
| plan.go | 17 | 0 | 0 |
| points.go | 18 | 10 | 0 |
| process.go | 13 | 0 | 0 |

Every file matched `func `, so the zeros are real. `points.go`'s 10 cookie hits are cookie *insertion points* (where to place a payload), not jar application. `intruder.go`'s single `session` hit is a comment.

For contrast, the crawler does apply the jar — `internal/crawler/session_gate.go:151` and `:249` both call `CookieHeader`.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do
Run an Intruder attack against an endpoint that requires a session. Every request in the attack is sent unauthenticated, and the attack's results describe the login wall rather than the endpoint.
acceptance_criteria: An Intruder attack against a host with cookies in the jar sends those cookies on each request, verified by a test asserting the Cookie header on the sent bytes. Whether the cookie being fuzzed is exempted from the jar (Burp's behaviour) is stated explicitly in the implementation.
close_reason: Fixed in 6427834. internal/web/intruder_cookies.go merges the jar into each spliced request inside the send path - after the splice, never before, because insertion points are byte spans into the base request and a header added to the base shifts every span after it. The jar OVERWRITES a same-named cookie in the capture rather than deferring to it (opposite of the Repeater's rule, and stated in the file comment: a Repeater request is bytes being edited now, an Intruder base request is a stale capture). Burp's exemption is implemented and stated explicitly per the acceptance criteria: a cookie the attack is fuzzing keeps its spliced value, taken by name from the selected PointCookieValue points' labels. RunView gains session_cookies {attached, exempt, jar_empty} - names only, no values, since they are session tokens; jar_empty is separate because an empty attached list also means 'every jar cookie was a fuzzed position'. Tests assert the Cookie header on the bytes the ORIGIN received (recordHeadsServer), not the jar or the report. Mutation: dropping applyJarCookies fails TestIntruderAttachesJarCookiesToEveryRequest ('0 of 3 requests carried a Cookie header'), TestIntruderRefreshesAStaleCookieFromTheJar and TestIntruderDoesNotOverwriteTheCookieItIsFuzzing; dropping only the exemption fails the last with 'sessid values seen = map[live-token:true], want the two payloads'.

comments.author: FixBackendTruth
comments.text:
SCOPE NOTE for the inventory (issue is closed/done, this is calibration).

ACCURATE AS FILED. The audit's evidence was exact — cookieHeaderFor's single call site, the per-file grep table over internal/intruder with 'func ' as a positive control, the correct reading that points.go's 10 cookie hits are insertion points and not jar application, and the crawler named as the contrasting case that does apply the jar. Nothing in it was wrong and nothing was missing. This is the calibration baseline: a P1 whose evidence let me go straight to implementation.

The acceptance criteria were also the right ones and drove the design, in particular 'whether the cookie being fuzzed is exempted from the jar is stated explicitly in the implementation'.

ONE NON-OBVIOUS CONSTRAINT the audit could not have known, worth recording for any future 'apply X to intruder requests' issue: insertion points are BYTE SPANS into the base request. Anything that adds or removes a header in the base shifts every span after it and the splice lands in the wrong place. So the merge has to run on the already-spliced bytes, inside the send closure — not on msg.Raw() before the attack is built, which is the obvious place and is wrong.

A JUDGEMENT CALL a reviewer may want to revisit: the jar OVERWRITES a same-named cookie already in the captured base request. That is the opposite of the Repeater's documented rule ('a header the operator wrote always wins', repeater_options.go). The reasoning, stated in internal/web/intruder_cookies.go: a Repeater request is bytes the operator is editing right now, whereas an Intruder base request is a capture from history whose Cookie header is a snapshot of a session that has probably since rotated — deferring to it is how the whole attack goes out unauthenticated while the jar holds a live session. Burp's docs support it ('the sessid cookie is updated when Intruder is fuzzing other parameters'). But it IS an intentional inconsistency between two tools in the same codebase, so it is a decision and not a fact.

NO REMAINING WORK. The UI needs nothing: cookies go out regardless of what the page does. RunView.session_cookies {attached, exempt, jar_empty} is available if intruder.tsx wants to show what the jar contributed — names only, never values, since they are session tokens and a report gets pasted into tickets.

title: proxy settings: no listener configuration at all — bind address/port, invisible proxying, redirect and per-listener certificate are unreachable
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD by AuditProxy (Proxy-screen parity audit, 2026-08-27).

Burp's "Proxy listeners" panel -- the first panel a migrating user opens on this
tool -- has no counterpart. burpsy shows the bind address as a read-only metric
and offers no way to add, edit or remove a listener.

## Burp-side evidence
