  Positive control on the same tree: `grep -rn "exchange_id" internal/web/ui/src/` → hits in
  `lib/types.ts` and `pages/repeater.tsx` (used at `:166,178,364`).

- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx:125` — a send appends only the result:
  `setHistory((current) => ({ ...current, [tab.id]: [...(current[tab.id] ?? []), result] }))`.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx:540-546` — the request editor is bound to `active.request`,
  the live draft, unconditionally. `viewIndex` (`:215`) affects only `result` (`:216`), which feeds the
  response editor at `:547-559`.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Compare. Having sent five variations of a header, the operator pages back to entry 2 to see the
response that behaved differently — and cannot see which variation entry 2 was. The comment at
`repeater.tsx:55-62` states the intent exactly ("the whole method of the tool is 'change one thing and
compare': overwriting the previous response destroys the half of the comparison you were about to
make"); the request half has the same problem the response half was fixed for.

## Secondary, same root cause

`history` is `useState` (`repeater.tsx:63`) and is excluded from `partialize`
(`internal/web/ui/src/lib/store.ts:321-335`, which persists `repeaterTabs`, `activeRepeaterTab`,
`repeaterGroups`). So the draft survives a reload and every response does not. Snapshotting the
request per entry and persisting entries would fix both; if persistence is deliberately declined, the
request snapshot still matters on its own.

## Cheap version

The server already returns `request_msg_id` per send. Storing the draft string in the history entry
client-side is enough for the comparison workflow and needs no backend change.
acceptance_criteria: Stepping through a tab's response history restores the request that produced each entry alongside its response.
close_reason: Added RepeaterHistoryEntry (RepeaterResult + client-side draft text snapshotted at send time). Request editor now renders the pinned history entry's snapshot (read-only, 'as written') instead of the live draft when stepping through history; Send is disabled while pinned to avoid firing the invisible live draft under a stale-looking request pane. History persistence across reloads left as an open follow-up (secondary note in the issue, not required by acceptance criteria). tsc --noEmit clean, bun test src/lib 172/0. Committed 2b69809, pushed to origin/ui-react-comparison.

title: intercept: a held request cannot be sent to Repeater or Intruder — the row menu offers only Forward and Drop
description:
## Claim
A held intercepted request cannot be sent to another tool. Proxy -> Intercept's row menu offers Forward and Drop only. Burp documents sending held messages to Repeater and Intruder as one of the four things intercept is for.

## Burp-side evidence
- `tools/proxy/intercept-messages.html` (Burp bundled docs), "The intercept feature enables you to perform the following useful actions": *"Intercept requests and modify them before forwarding them to the server. Release a selection of requests at once. **Send interesting requests to Burp's other tools, such as Repeater or Intruder, for further testing.** Drop one or more requests to prevent them from reaching the server."*
- Same page: *"You can also right-click to access different context menus in the message editor, or the list of intercepted messages."*

## burpsy-side evidence
- The held-message row menu is Forward and Drop only: `pages/intercept.tsx:728-753` — `menuGroups={(row) => [{ id: "intercept", actions: [{ id: "forward", ... }, { id: "drop", ... }] }]}`.
- The shared action surface is not imported on this page: `grep -c useExchangeActions pages/intercept.tsx` -> **0**. Same-file positive control: `grep -c import pages/intercept.tsx` -> **13**. `grep -n 'sendToRepeater|Send to' pages/intercept.tsx` -> no hits.
- Contrast the four surfaces that do have it: `pages/history.tsx:1012`, `pages/sitemap.tsx:548`, `pages/wshistory.tsx:213` all pass `actions.menu(row)` from `lib/actions.ts:782`.
- Note the held message is not yet a stored exchange, so `lib/actions.ts`'s `Exchange`-shaped menu does not apply unchanged — the hand-off needs the held bytes, which the page already has as `row.raw` (used at `pages/intercept.tsx:742`).

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do
Hold a request, decide it deserves proper work, and push it to Repeater. Today the only path is: forward it, go to HTTP history, find the row, then send from there — which also loses any edit made in the intercept buffer.
acceptance_criteria: The held-message row menu and the held-bytes editor offer send-to-Repeater and send-to-Intruder, carrying the held bytes (including any edits in the buffer) rather than requiring the message be forwarded first.
close_reason: Closed STALE: the claim predates the held-row menu expansion. intercept.tsx:473-607 heldMenu() now offers Send to Repeater (copies row.raw to a Repeater tab without resolving the hold), Send to Comparer A/B, Send to Decoder, Copy URL/curl/to-file, Add host to scope, Open in browser, plus Forward/Drop. Only the Intruder handoff is absent, and :459-461 documents why it is deliberate: Intruder splices into a stored message id, which a held message does not have. Verified against HEAD 325905b by source read; no code change needed.

title: logger: proxy traffic is excluded, so the tool log is not a unified traffic log
description:
## Claim
The tool log excludes proxy traffic, so it is not the unified traffic log Burp Logger is.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/logger/index.html` — the contrast with HTTP history is the tool's stated identity:
> "Burp Logger records **all** the HTTP traffic that Burp Suite generates in real-time. […] By default, Logger displays traffic generated by **all the tools** in Burp Suite. This includes modified requests, and requests sent by extensions. **By contrast, the HTTP history only displays traffic from a browser that is proxied through Burp.**"

`BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md` §4.10: "Top = Unified traffic log table across all tools".

Burp's capture filter then has an explicit per-tool axis including Proxy (`tools/logger/filter/capture.html`, "Capture by tool"), which only makes sense because Proxy is captured by default.

## burpsy-side evidence
The page states the exclusion itself — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/logger.tsx:410`:
> "Repeater, Intruder, Scanner and the crawler record every request they send here, **apart from proxy history**."

The tool set is `toollog.ToolAll`, seeded into the histogram at `internal/web/api_toolkit.go:942-945`; the page's tool filter and capture checkboxes are both derived from that histogram (`pages/logger.tsx:109`, `:324-334`), so whatever is not a `toollog.Tool` cannot appear.

The page is also titled "Tool log" (`pages/logger.tsx:247`), not Logger — the naming is consistent with the narrower scope.

## Classification
UX DIVERGENCE, arguably deliberate — but undeclared. Unlike the Comparer's word-level mode, there is no statement that proxy traffic is excluded *by choice*; line 410 reads as a description of current coverage, not a decision.

## Decision needed before code
1. Include proxy traffic as a `toollog.Tool`, making the page a real unified log. Then the existing per-tool capture axis (`pages/logger.tsx:320-335`) already gives the operator the switch to turn it off, and the two-axis model matches Burp's. Cost: proxy volume dominates the bounded log, so the eviction counter (`Dropped()`) becomes load-bearing.
2. Keep the exclusion and declare it — rename the concept consistently and say in the page copy that proxy traffic lives in HTTP history by design, so a Burp user stops looking for it here.

Worth settling alongside the message-viewer issue, since both bear on whether this page is Logger or something narrower.

## What an operator cannot do
See a browser request and the tool request it provoked in one ordered list — the view Burp uses to answer "what did the suite actually send, in what order".
acceptance_criteria: Either proxy traffic appears in the log as its own tool with a capture toggle, or the page states that proxy traffic is excluded by design and directs the operator to HTTP history. Decided and recorded either way.

title: logger: TLS flag is dropped from the wire, so Copy URL emits http:// for HTTPS on non-443 ports
description:
## Claim
The tool log's TLS flag is recorded but dropped from the wire shape, so Logger's Copy URL and Copy as curl emit `http://` for an HTTPS service on any port other than 443.

## Burp-side evidence
Burp Logger's table and its copy actions carry the real scheme; `tools/logger/entries.html` describes copying column data and sending entries to other tools, all of which require the correct URL. There is no guessing step in Burp because the protocol is part of the logged item.

## burpsy-side evidence
The field exists on the record — `internal/toollog/toollog.go:86`:
```go
TLS    bool
```

It is absent from the wire projection — `internal/web/api_toolkit.go:835-854`, the full `toolLogEntry` struct: `id, tool, host, port, method, path, status, response_len, started_ms, duration_ms, error`. No `tls`.

So the frontend guesses, and says so — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/logger.tsx:14-23`:
```ts
/**
 * A logged row records a request one of burpsy's own tools sent. The log carries
 * no TLS flag, so the scheme is inferred from the port — the only honest guess
 * available, and why the URL actions say "as logged".
 */
function rowUrl(row: ToolLogRow): string {
  const scheme = row.port === 443 ? "https" : "http";
```
Consumers: "Copy URL (as logged)" (`pages/logger.tsx:358-367`), "Copy as curl (request line only)" (`:368-375`), and the detail-pane heading (`:203-205`).

The comment is accurate about the wire and is the reason this is a small fix rather than a design question: the honest guess was the right call given the shape, and the shape is wrong.

## Concrete failure
A request to `https://api.example:8443/v1/x` logged by Repeater renders and copies as `http://api.example:8443/v1/x`. Pasting that into a terminal or a browser hits the wrong scheme; `curl -i -X GET "http://api.example:8443/v1/x"` against a TLS listener fails or is redirected, and the operator debugs their copy rather than their target.

## Classification
Correctness defect. One field already in the struct, not projected.

## What an operator cannot do
Trust the URL the Logger hands them for any HTTPS service not on 443 — which is most internal and staging targets.
acceptance_criteria: toolLogEntry carries the entry's TLS flag, rowUrl uses it instead of inferring from the port, and the "as logged" hedge is dropped from the action labels. A test asserts an https-on-8443 entry copies as https.
close_reason: Fixed in c6d9339. toolLogEntry gains 'tls', set from e.TLS in toolLogEntryView - the single projection both /api/tools/log and /api/dashboard go through, which is the arrangement that exists because started_ms once went missing from one of them. The audit was exactly right that the field was already on the record and merely not projected. Mutation: dropping 'TLS: e.TLS' fails TestToolLogWireCarriesTheTLSFlag ('the https-on-8443 row is projected with tls=false, so Copy URL emits http:// for it') and TestDashboardActivityCarriesTheTLSFlagToo. The test drives an https-on-8443 row AND a plaintext-on-8080 row so a projection that hardcoded either answer fails. UI half open (logger.tsx is owned by another agent this session): rowUrl should read row.tls instead of inferring from the port, and the 'as logged' hedge on the two copy actions and the detail-pane heading can go with it.

comments.author: FixBackendTruth
comments.text:
SCOPE NOTE for the inventory (issue is closed/done, this is calibration).

ACCURATE AS FILED, AND CORRECTLY SIZED. The audit called it 'small, one field already in the struct, not projected' and that is exactly what it was: two lines of production code. It also correctly judged that the frontend's port-based guess was the right call given the shape and that the shape was the bug. Nothing to re-scope.

Use this one as the low end of the calibration range: a P2 correctness defect where the record already held the truth and only the projection dropped it. If other issues in the inventory match that description — field present on the internal type, absent from the wire struct — they are the same size.

The one thing I would add to the filed evidence: the fix belongs in toolLogEntryView (api_dashboard.go:307), the SINGLE projection that both /api/tools/log and /api/dashboard go through. That funnel exists because started_ms once went missing from one of the two, and its comment says so. Any future 'field X is missing from the tool log wire' issue is one line there, and the test should assert both routes.

REMAINING (UI, not mine, and small): logger.tsx:14-23's rowUrl should read row.tls instead of inferring from the port, and the 'as logged' hedge can then come off the two copy actions (:358-375) and the detail-pane heading (:203-205). Note the ordering — the hedge is currently HONEST and must not be removed before rowUrl actually reads the flag, or the labels would start overstating what the page knows.

title: intruder: payload files can only be loaded from a path on the burpsy server, so an operator cannot use a wordlist from their own machine
description:
Intruder's file payload type takes a path that is resolved on the burpsy **server**. There is no way
to load a wordlist from the machine the operator is sitting at, and no upload route exists.

This is a separate concern from *which* wordlists ship (that is the licensing decision already filed):
even with a perfect corpus available locally, an operator cannot get their own list into an attack
against a remote burpsy.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/payload-lists.html`
and `.../payload-types.html` — the payload options box has **Add**, **Load ...**, **Remove**, **Clear**
buttons; `Load ...` opens a file chooser on the operator's own filesystem. Burp is a desktop app, so
local and server are the same machine there — but Burp's *user* settings page is explicit that
uploading lists is a first-class action:
`.../configure-attack/settings.html` — "To configure Burp Intruder user settings for startup and
closing behavior, and **to upload payload lists**, go to the Intruder page in the Settings dialog."
The spec records the buttons at `/root/burp-re/BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md:170`.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:816-828` — the only file control is a text input for a
  server-side path, and the hint says so:

      <Field label="Server file path" hint="File must exist on server; blank lines skipped">
        ... placeholder="/tmp/payloads.txt or ./wordlists/sqli.txt"

- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:508-510` — the wire form is
  `{ type: "file", filename: ... }`.
- `internal/intruder/payload.go:208` — "FileSource is the filename for `{"type":"file"}` — payloads
  from server file, one per line"; resolved at `internal/intruder/payload.go:259` and `:363-366`.
- No upload route exists. `grep -rni "upload|multipart" internal/web/server.go` returns a single hit —
  `internal/web/server.go:175`, a comment about the 16 MiB body cap ("runaway upload cannot exhaust
  memory"). Positive control on the same file: `grep -n "intruder" internal/web/server.go` → `:263`,
  `:742`, `:743`.
- Nor is there a file input in the UI: `grep -rn "type=\"file\"" internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx`
  → no output; positive control on the same file, `grep -c "Input" internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx`
  → non-zero (the page is full of them).

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Use their own wordlist. burpsy runs as a server; when that server is a container, a VM or a jump host
— which is the normal deployment — the operator's `~/wordlists/usernames.txt` is not on it, and the
only workaround is an out-of-band copy (scp, a volume mount) before every attack. Combined with the
zero bundled corpora, Intruder ships with no reachable payload source other than typing lines into a
textarea.

## Note on the decision boundary

Do not fold this into the wordlist-licensing issue. That one asks *what content burpsy ships*; this one
asks *how an operator supplies content at all*, and it stands even if the answer there is "ship
nothing". The wordlist issue's second proposed outcome — a shared wordlist manager, since
`/api/discovery` already takes a wordlist path — would resolve both if it includes an upload or
browse-the-server path picker. Whoever takes that one should read this.
acceptance_criteria: An operator can supply a payload list from their own machine — by upload or an equivalent — without shell access to the burpsy host.

title: intruder: Grep - match takes one expression and reports a boolean, not Burp's expression list with a per-expression occurrence-count column
description:
Burp's Grep - match takes a **list** of expressions and adds one results column per expression,
counting occurrences per response. burpsy takes a single expression and reports one boolean per
attempt.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html`,
under **Grep - match**:

> **Flag responses matching these expressions** - Specify a list of expressions to flag. By default,
> the expressions list shows some common error strings that are useful when fuzzing.
>
> During the attack, Burp adds a results column for each expression in the list. This records the
> number of times the expression is found in the response. To identify results with the expression,
> click on the column header to sort the results.

Also in the same section, and equally absent on the burpsy side: **Match type** (simple string /
regex), **Case sensitive match**, and **Exclude HTTP headers**.

## burpsy-side evidence

Single expression, boolean answer, all the way down:

- `internal/web/api_tools.go:355-356` — `GrepMatch *string` and `GrepExtract *string`. Scalars, not
  lists.
- `internal/web/api_tools.go:736-752` (`buildGrep`) — compiles exactly one pattern for each.
- `internal/intruder/engine.go:76-83` — `Grep{MatchRe, ExtractRe *regexp.Regexp}`; one each.
- `internal/intruder/engine.go:89-101` (`run`) — `MatchRe.Match(raw)` returns a bool. No occurrence
  count anywhere.
- `internal/intruder/engine.go:227` — `Attempt.GrepMatched *bool`.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:1049-1062` — one input per grep field.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:323` — the results column renders a badge reading "match",
  not a number.

There is no case-sensitivity or exclude-headers option: `Grep.run` is handed the whole raw response
including the header block (`engine.go:89`), and case behaviour is whatever the operator encodes in
the pattern (`(?i)`).

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Fuzz with more than one indicator at a time. Burp's default fuzzing workflow is to flag a dozen error
strings at once and sort by whichever column lights up; here the operator must either union them into
one regex — losing the ability to tell *which* one matched, since the answer is a single bool — or run
the attack once per indicator. Counting occurrences is also unavailable, so "this response mentions
`root:` eleven times" and "once" look identical.

## Related, filed separately

The labelling defect on these same two fields (they are regexes described as literal strings) is a
distinct issue. This issue is about arity and the missing per-expression options, and it should be
designed together with that one since both touch the same wire fields.

Burp's **Grep - payloads** options (case sensitivity, exclude headers, match against pre-URL-encoded
payloads) are also absent — burpsy detects reflection as a bare boolean at
`internal/intruder/engine.go:224` (`Attempt.Reflected`) with no options — and are filed separately.
acceptance_criteria: Grep - match accepts a list of expressions with match-type, case-sensitivity and exclude-headers options, and results carry one occurrence-count column per expression.

title: intruder: a network failure is never retried — no retry count and no pause-before-retry exist
description:
A network failure on one Intruder request is permanent. There is no retry count and no pause-before-
retry, so a transient error turns into a counted `failed` attempt and a hole in the results.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html`,
under **Error handling**:

> **Number of retries on network failure** - Specify the number of times Burp retries a request when a
> failure occurs. Intermittent network failures are common when testing, so it is best to retry the
> request several times.
>
> **Pause before retry** - Specify the time (in milliseconds) that Burp waits before retrying a failed
> request.

Burp's own guidance is that this is the common case ("intermittent network failures are common when
testing"), which is why both knobs are defaults-on rather than expert options.

## burpsy-side evidence

- `internal/web/api_tools.go:614-628` — the `send` closure is one `auth.Send` per request with a
  per-send timeout and no retry loop:

      send := func(raw []byte) (intruder.Sent, error) {
          ... sctx, cancel = context.WithTimeout(ctx, timeout) ...
          res, err := auth.Send(sctx, raw)
          if err != nil { return intruder.Sent{}, err }
          ...
      }

- `internal/intruder/engine.go` — `Run` records the error against the attempt and moves on; the error
  is grouped into `ErrorBucket` (`engine.go:245`) and counted in `report.Failed` (`:240`).
- `internal/web/api_tools.go:348-364` — `intruderRunReq` has no retry or retry-delay field.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:1043-1065` — the Settings tab has no such control.

Absence grep:

    $ grep -rli "retries" internal/intruder internal/web/api_tools.go internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx
    (no output)

Positive control from the same invocation over the same paths: `grep -rli "baseline" ...` →
`internal/intruder/engine_test.go`.

Note what *does* exist and is not a substitute: `intruder.RateLimit.WithAutoThrottle`
(`internal/web/api_tools.go:420-428`, `internal/intruder/limit.go`) slows the attack down in response
to configured *statuses*. That is Burp's throttling behaviour, not its retry behaviour — it never
re-sends the failed request.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Get a complete result set over a flaky link or against a target with connection limits. A 2,000-
request attack across a VPN drops an arbitrary handful of attempts, and because the payload behind a
failed ordinal is not displayed either, the operator cannot even tell which payloads were never
actually tested. The report is honest that they failed — `report.failed` and the grouped `errors`
table (`pages/intruder.tsx:240-257`) — but the only remedy is re-running the whole attack.

## Note

Retry interacts with the rate limiter: a retry must consume a token from the same
`intruder.RateLimiter` rather than bypass it, or the retry path becomes a way to exceed the pool's
rps. Worth stating in the implementation.
acceptance_criteria: Retry count and pause-before-retry are configurable per attack, retries consume the same rate limiter as first sends, and the report distinguishes an attempt that succeeded after retry from one that never succeeded.

title: intruder: no Make unmodified baseline request, so no attack has a base response to compare against
description:
Burp's `Make unmodified baseline request` issues the template request with every payload position at
its original value, as item 0 of the results, so every attack response has something to be compared
against. burpsy has no equivalent.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html`,
under **Attack results**:

> **Make unmodified baseline request** - Set the attack to issue the template request with all payload
> positions set to their base values, in addition to the configured attack requests. The request shows
> as item 0 in the results table. This is useful to provide a base response against which to compare
> the attack responses.

The spec records the control's own id: `/root/burp-re/BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md:173` —
`setName("intruderAttackConfigSettingsMakeUnmodifiedBaselineRequest")`.

## burpsy-side evidence

Absent from the engine, the wire contract and the UI:

- `internal/web/api_tools.go:348-364` — `intruderRunReq` has no baseline field. The full field list is
  `msg_id, target, all, point_index, payloads, mode, points, payload_sets, payload_sources,
  payload_rules, max_payloads, grep_match, grep_extract, pool, auto_throttle, rps, max_in_flight,
  max_requests, timeout_ms`.
- `internal/intruder/engine.go:232-249` — `AttackReport` has no baseline field; `Attempts` are plan
  ordinals only, and ordinals start at the plan's first combination.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:1043-1065` — the Settings tab contains only the two grep
  fields.

Absence grep:

    $ grep -rli "baseline" internal/intruder internal/web/api_tools.go internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx
    internal/intruder/engine_test.go

The single hit is a test, not an implementation, and it is the positive control for this grep: the
pattern does match in this path set, so the empty result for the non-test files is real.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Tell an interesting response from the application's normal one. burpsy's result buckets group by
status, length and reflection (`internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:209-234`), which is a good
substitute for eyeballing a table — but with no baseline row, the operator cannot tell whether the
largest bucket *is* the normal response or whether every single response differs from the unattacked
request. For a single-position sniper over a login form, "all 500 responses were 200/4.1 kB" means
nothing without knowing what the untouched request returns.

## Note on shape

This composes with the honest-accounting style already in the report: a baseline attempt would be one
extra send with `ApplyAll` given no payloads, recorded as ordinal 0 and excluded from the bucket
counts (or shown as its own row) so it cannot inflate `sent`. It needs `Attempt`/`ResultBucket` to
distinguish "baseline" from "attempt 0", which today are the same integer.
acceptance_criteria: An opt-in baseline setting issues the template request with all positions at their base values, reported as its own result distinguishable from attempt 0 and excluded from bucket counts.

title: intruder: the request-count badge and over-budget warning use hard-coded counts for the file, dates and custom-iterator payload types
description:
Intruder's header shows a request-count badge and raises an over-budget warning when the count
exceeds the cap. For three of the seven payload types the count it uses is a hard-coded constant, not
a computation, so the badge is wrong and the warning cannot fire.

## burpsy-side evidence

`internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:425-456` (`setSizes`):

    if (t === "file") return 1;
    ...
    if (t === "dates") {
      ...
      return 10; // approximate; server computes exact
    }
    if (t === "custom_iterator") return 4; // approximate

Those values feed straight into the displayed estimate and the guard:

- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:457` — `estimateRequests(mode, selected.length, setSizes)`.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:561-563` — the header badge:
  `{formatCount(estimate.count)} request{...}`.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:551` — `const overBudget = estimate.count > maxRequests;`
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:574-583` — the warning notice, shown only when
  `overBudget`.

The comments are honest that the numbers are approximations, but the UI presents them as a count and
uses them as a guard.

## Worked cases

- **Custom iterator** with three lines of 20 items each is 8,000 combinations. Badge reads
  `4 requests`. Cap is 1,000 (`intruder.tsx:356`). No warning fires; the server truncates at the cap
  and the report comes back marked `truncated` — the operator learns after the fact.
- **File** payload type pointing at a 50,000-line wordlist. Badge reads `1 request`.
- **Dates** across a year at step 1 is 366 payloads. Badge reads `10 requests`.

The engine does the arithmetic correctly — `intruder.NewAttackPlan` /
`internal/web/api_tools.go:601` and the bound at `:566-570` — so this is a display and guard defect,
not a sending defect.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/payload-types.html`
— Burp shows the payload count per set and the total request count for the attack, derived from the
configured generator, for every payload type including the file and date/iterator generators.

## Classification

UX DIVERGENCE. Not a decorative control — the value the operator types does reach the server and is
acted on; it is the *feedback* about that value that is fabricated.

## What an operator cannot do

Size an attack before launching it. The one number the header exists to provide is silently wrong for
file, date and custom-iterator sets, and the over-budget warning that exists to stop an accidental
outage cannot trigger for exactly the generator types most likely to be large.

## Note

Two of the three are computable client-side without server help: `custom_iterator` is the product of
the per-line item counts (the UI already parses those lines at `intruder.tsx:521`), and `dates` is
`floor(days_between/step)+1`. `file` genuinely is not knowable client-side — the honest options are to
display "unknown" and suppress the badge/warning rather than `1`, or add a server-side count probe.
acceptance_criteria: The estimate is computed for custom_iterator and dates, and file sets display an explicit unknown rather than 1; the over-budget warning fires for an oversized set of any type.
close_reason:
Done in 0fe8857, taking the honest option the issue's own Note sanctions for the file case.

- `custom_iterator` — was the constant 4, now `customIteratorSize`: the product of the per-line item counts. The issue's worked case (three lines of 20) reads 8,000 and trips the over-budget warning. The same parser now builds the request body, so the badge and what is sent cannot disagree — previously a blank line sent an empty slot the estimate did not account for.
- `dates` — was the constant 10, now `dateSetSize`: inclusive of both ends, stepping in whole days. 2024-01-01..2024-12-31 step 1 reads 366.
- `file` — was the constant 1. A server-side file is not knowable in the browser, so its size is now `null` and the whole estimate is presented as a floor: the badge reads '≥ N requests' with tone and tooltip saying so, the empty state says 'at least N requests planned', and a notice states that the cap has not been checked against the file's real length and that the server will mark the report truncated if it is reached. The per-set label reads '(unknown)' rather than '(1)'.
- The over-budget guard fires whenever the known floor exceeds the cap — including a floor that a file set contributed to — but its *silence* no longer implies safety, and the UI says which of the two it is. `estimateRequests` returns `exact` and every consumer branches on it.
- `canRun` had to change too: it required every set size > 0, and an unknown (null) size would have read as empty and blocked the launch of any file-backed attack.
- An unknown size in a set the mode never reads (sniper and battering ram read set 0 only) does not make the estimate a floor. Pinned by test.

Tests: 32 new in src/lib/types.tools.test.ts covering dateSetSize (both ends, stepping, reversed range, unparseable bound, non-positive step), customIteratorSize (the 8,000 case, empty iterator, blank-item filtering) and estimateRequests (exact, floor, unread-set, no-sets).

Where this stops short of the literal acceptance wording: the warning still cannot fire for an oversized *file* set, because nothing in the browser knows the file's length. The issue's Note names the two options — display unknown and suppress the fabricated number, or add a server-side count probe — and this is the first. A count probe on /api/intruder would close the remaining gap and needs a Go change; worth filing if you want the guard to cover file sets.

title: intruder: the Resource pool tab cannot select a saved resource pool, although /api/pools and the intruder run endpoint both support one
description:
burpsy has a complete named-resource-pool implementation: four routes, a registry, per-attack
resolution, and an editor UI. Intruder has a sub-tab called **Resource pool**. The two are not
connected — the tab is an inline limits form and never sends a pool name.

## Burp-side evidence

`/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources/Documentation/burp/documentation/desktop/tools/intruder/configure-attack/resource-pool.html`
— the Resource pool sub-tab lists the existing pools with a selectable entry per pool, plus "Create
new resource pool". Selecting a pool is how an attack is bound to shared engagement limits.

## burpsy-side evidence

The feature exists and works:

- `internal/web/api_pools.go` — GET/POST `/api/pools`, PUT/DELETE `/api/pools/{name}`; registered at
  `internal/web/server.go` alongside the other config routes.
- `internal/web/api_tools.go:359` — `Pool *string \`json:"pool"\`` on `intruderRunReq`.
- `internal/web/api_tools.go:382-400` (`s.intruderLimits`) — a named pool resolves through
  `s.pools.Limit(...)`, and an unknown name is deliberately refused with a 404 rather than silently
  falling back. The doc comment above it explains exactly why this matters: the old behaviour would
  "make a deleted or renamed pool run the attack at whatever inline default was in play, while the
  report said the pool's name — an attack running faster than the operator authorised".
- Editable in the UI, but only from Settings: `internal/web/ui/src/pages/settings.tsx:1998-2050`
  (`PoolDialog`, and the panel doc comment names it "Burp's configPanelResourcePools"), backed by
  `internal/web/ui/src/lib/data.pools.ts:90-116`.

The Intruder tab does not use it:

- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:592` — `<TabsTrigger value="pool">Resource pool</TabsTrigger>`.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:997-1040` — the tab's contents are three inline number
  fields: Max requests, Max concurrent requests, Requests per second. No pool list, no pool selector.
- `internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:489-501` — the request body sent to `/api/intruder/run`
  carries `max_requests`, `max_in_flight` and optionally `rps`. There is no `pool` key.

Absence check on the whole UI source: `grep -rn "api/pools" internal/web/ui/src/` →
`lib/data.pools.ts` (4 hits) and `pages/settings.tsx:2005` (a comment). No Intruder hit. Positive
control from the same sweep: `grep -rn "api/intruder" internal/web/ui/src/` →
`lib/data.tools.ts:97,103`.

## Classification

UX DIVERGENCE — a working backend feature with no route to it from the screen Burp puts it on.

## What an operator cannot do

Bind an attack to a saved pool. Having created a "2 req/s, 4 concurrent" engagement pool in Settings,
the operator must retype those numbers into the Intruder tab for every attack, and the report will
not name the pool. Worse, `intruderLimits` refuses a request that carries both a pool name and inline
limits (`api_tools.go:384-390`), so a client cannot simply add `pool` to the existing body — the
inline fields must become mutually exclusive with the selector.

## Note

The tab's current heading text is "An attack is always bounded; these are the limits the engine
enforces" (`intruder.tsx:1001`), which is accurate about what the tab does. The divergence is that
the tab is *named* after a Burp concept it does not expose.
acceptance_criteria: The Intruder Resource pool tab lists the saved pools from GET /api/pools and lets an operator bind the attack to one, sending pool on the run request, with the inline limit fields disabled while a pool is selected.
close_reason:
Done in 0fe8857 (no Go change — /api/pools and the run endpoint already supported it).

The Resource pool tab is now two cards:
- 'Saved resource pool' — a Select over GET /api/pools via the existing `usePools` hook, defaulting to 'Inline limits (no saved pool)'. Loading, request failure (ErrorNotice with retry) and no-pools-saved are three distinct states, not one empty select. Choosing a pool shows what it enforces (concurrency, delay, whether automatic throttling is on), read from the pool object rather than restated.
- 'Inline limits' — Max requests, concurrency, rate. Selecting a pool disables concurrency and rate, shows the pool's concurrency in the disabled field, and says why. Max requests stays live and the heading says so: it bounds the attack's size, not its rate, and intruderLimits does not include it in the exclusion.

The run body follows the exclusion exactly: with a pool it sends `pool` and omits `max_in_flight`/`rps`; without one it sends the inline pair as before. Nothing is sent that the server would refuse.

One thing beyond the acceptance criteria, from reading intruderLimits: a persisted pool name whose pool has since been deleted or renamed would fail the launch with a 404. The tab now warns before that happens, naming the pool and saying the server refuses a name it cannot resolve.

NOT done: 'Create new resource pool' from inside this tab. Pools remain created and edited under Settings, and the empty state points there.

title: session: the cookie jar is read-only — no way to edit, remove or empty cookies
description:
## Claim
The cookie jar is read-only: there is no way to edit a cookie, remove one, or empty the jar.

## Burp-side evidence
`settings/sessions/index.html`, "Managing the cookie jar":
> "To manage the contents of the cookie jar, click Open cookie jar. You can **edit cookies manually, remove cookies from the jar, or empty the jar altogether**."

## burpsy-side evidence
The endpoint is GET-only — `internal/web/api_session.go:958-962`:
```go
func (s *Server) handleSessionCookies(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodGet {
        http.Error(w, "Method not allowed", http.StatusMethodNotAllowed)
        return
    }
```
and it is the only cookie route — `internal/web/server.go:780` registers `/api/session/cookies` and nothing else under it (the neighbouring session routes are `/api/session/rules`, `/api/session/rules/`, `/api/session/login` at `server.go:778-781`).

The store exposes no mutator: `CookieJarManager` has `CookieHeader` (`internal/session/session.go:664`), `AbsorbSetCookie` (`:675`) and `Jars` (`:570`). No delete, no clear, no set.

The page renders a plain read-only table — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/session.tsx:1025-1040`, three cells (Authority, Name, Value) with no controls and no per-row actions.

## Why this matters more here than it would in Burp
`internal/session/session.go:626-638` records that cookie attributes are dropped and cookies therefore "persist for the life of the process". That is a stated, deliberate simplification — but it means a stale or wrong cookie in the jar cannot expire out and cannot be removed either, so the only remedy available to the operator is restarting the process, which costs them their captured traffic.

The two together are worse than either alone, which is why the read-only jar is filed even though the attribute-dropping is deliberate and disclosed.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do
Clear a poisoned session. A jar holding a logged-out or wrong-user cookie will keep attaching it to every Repeater send, and the only way out is a restart.
acceptance_criteria: The cookie jar table supports editing a cookie's value, deleting a single cookie, and emptying the jar, each reaching the coordinator's jar and reflected in the next request that would carry the cookie. Emptying the jar is confirmed, matching the existing destructive-action pattern on this page.

title: collaborator: no "Insert Collaborator payload" action in Repeater or Intruder
description:
## Claim
There is no "Insert Collaborator payload" action in Repeater or Intruder, so an out-of-band payload can only reach a request by the operator pasting it in by hand.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/collaborator/index.html`, "Generating payloads" — this is the primary insertion route, listed before the bulk-copy one:
> "You can directly insert Collaborator payloads into any request that is open in Burp Repeater. Right-click on the request and select **Insert Collaborator payload**.
> You can automatically insert Collaborator payloads into a Burp Intruder attack. For more information, see Payload types - Collaborator payloads."

`tools/collaborator/getting-started.html` makes it step 4 of the canonical manual OOB workflow:
> "Go to the Repeater tab. Highlight the URL in the Referer header, right-click, and select Insert Collaborator payload. This replaces the Referer URL with a URL that points to the Collaborator server."

## burpsy-side evidence
Absence-grep on the three files the action would live in, with same-file positive control:
```
$ grep -rn "collab\|Collab" internal/web/ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx \
      internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx internal/web/ui/src/lib/actions.ts
(no output)

$ grep -c "Repeater" internal/web/ui/src/pages/repeater.tsx
67
```
All three files are readable; the zero is real.

The context-menu send group (`internal/web/ui/src/lib/actions.ts:366-371`) is Repeater / Intruder / Comparer A / Comparer B / Decoder — no Collaborator entry, and no in-editor insertion action anywhere.

Minting works and is reachable, but only as clipboard: `internal/web/ui/src/pages/collaborator.tsx:144-158` mints one address and copies it (`copyToClipboard(payload.address)` at `:150`). The operator then switches tab and pastes.

Intruder payload types: no Collaborator payload type — `internal/web/ui/src/lib/types.tools.ts` carries `PAYLOAD_LAYERS` for payload *processing*, and the generator set has no OOB member.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## What works today, for scoping
The rest of the manual OOB loop is functional and should not be re-implemented: mint (`api_collaborator.go` mint handler), auto-refreshing interactions every 5s (`internal/web/ui/src/lib/data.collab.ts:56,68,173` — tighter than Burp's 60s auto-poll), the interaction table with Burp's own columns (`pages/collaborator.tsx:284`), and a detail pane carrying the correlation id, the client-IP interpretation and the raw request (`pages/collaborator.tsx:321-333`). The divergence in what "Poll now" means is disclosed on the wire itself (`internal/web/api_collaborator.go:83-85`).

So this issue is only the insertion half.

## What an operator cannot do
Put a payload into a request without leaving the request. Every blind-SSRF or OOB test is: open Collaborator, mint, switch to Repeater, paste, switch back — and for Intruder, there is no route at all, so an OOB payload cannot be swept across a parameter list.
acceptance_criteria: Repeater offers an action that mints a payload and inserts it at the cursor or over the selection in the request editor, and Intruder offers a Collaborator payload generator that mints a fresh address per request. Both refuse with a stated reason when no interaction server is configured, rather than inserting a placeholder.

title: decoder: gzip and deflate are missing from the Decoder dropdown though the engine and handler support them
description:
## Claim
The Decoder's dropdown omits gzip and deflate, which the decode engine and its own HTTP handler both support — and one consequence is that a warning notice on the Decoder page can never fire.

## Burp-side evidence
`tools/decoder.html`, "Operations":
> "The following decode and encode functions are available: URL. HTML. Base64. ASCII hex. Hex. Octal. Binary. **GZIP**."

## burpsy-side evidence — the capability exists
`internal/tools/codec.go:83-85`:
```go
func AllLayers() []Layer {
    return []Layer{LayerURL, LayerHTML, LayerBase64, LayerBase64URL, LayerHex, LayerGzip, LayerDeflate, LayerJWT}
}
```
Both have full decode arms — `LayerGzip` at `internal/tools/codec.go:137` and `:185`, `LayerDeflate` at `:139` and `:195` (the latter documented at `codec.go:41-43` as trying zlib-wrapped first, then raw), with an inflate bound at `codec.go:91` (`MaxInflate`).

The handler accepts them: `decodeLayer` (`internal/web/api_toolkit.go:1072-1091`) resolves any name through `tools.ParseLayer` and returns the codec's partial-decompression flag, so `POST /api/tools/decode` with `{"encoding":"gzip"}` works today. The handler comment at `api_toolkit.go:1066-1071` records that this was the fix for gzip/deflate previously falling through a hand-rolled switch.

## burpsy-side evidence — the page cannot reach it
The dropdown is built from a hand-maintained frontend list, `internal/web/ui/src/lib/data.workbench.ts:41`:
```ts
export const DECODE_LAYERS = ["url", "html", "base64", "base64url", "hex", "jwt", "ascii"] as const;
```
consumed by `valuesFor("decode")` at `internal/web/ui/src/pages/decoder.tsx:22`, which is the only source of the Select's options (`pages/decoder.tsx:97-103`). gzip and deflate are absent.

Verified across the whole UI tree rather than the file expected, with positive control:
```
$ cd internal/web/ui/src && grep -rn "gzip\|deflate" --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx .
lib/types.tools.ts:36:export const PAYLOAD_LAYERS = ["url", "html", "base64", "base64url", "hex", "gzip", "deflate"] as const;

$ grep -rn "base64url" --include=*.ts --include=*.tsx . | head -3
ui/typed-views.tsx:128: ...
lib/types.tools.ts:36: ...
lib/data.workbench.ts:39: ...
```
So the same two layers *are* offered elsewhere in the UI — `PAYLOAD_LAYERS` at `lib/types.tools.ts:36`, for Intruder payload processing. The build can gzip-decode inside an Intruder payload chain and not in the tool built for peeling layers.

## Knock-on: unreachable UI
`smartDecode`'s step list is base64 / url / hex / html only (`internal/web/api_toolkit.go:1183-1191`), so neither the explicit path nor smart detect can produce a `partial` flag from this page. The "This stream only partly decompressed…" notice at `internal/web/ui/src/pages/decoder.tsx:186-192` is therefore dead code — it is well-written and says the right thing, and nothing can make it appear.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP — reachability, not implementation. The fix is two entries in a frontend list, plus deciding whether smart detect should attempt decompression.

## Also absent everywhere
Octal and Binary, from Burp's list above, are not in the codec table at all. Mentioned for completeness; not part of this claim, since they are a genuine implementation gap rather than a wiring one.

## What an operator cannot do
Hand-decode a gzipped response body in the Decoder — the exact "unpack layers of encoding" task the tool exists for — while the same engine will do it one page over.
acceptance_criteria: gzip and deflate are selectable as Decoder steps and decode correctly, and a truncated stream renders the existing partial-decompression notice — proving that notice is now reachable. Whether smart detect also attempts decompression is decided and recorded either way.
close_reason: Done in 7b09060. DECODE_LAYERS gains gzip and deflate; ENCODE_ENCODINGS gains them too, since codec.go's Encode has a case for each. LayerJWT stays out of the encode list because it is decode-only by construction. The capability was fully present — AllLayers() returned both, ParseLayer resolved gzip/gz and deflate/zlib — and no operator could reach it, which is this project's signature bug shape. Side effect worth knowing: decoder.tsx's 'this stream only partly decompressed' notice draws its flag from the gzip/deflate path, so it could never fire before and can now. EVIDENCE: I could not run the web-package test because another agent is mid-write on internal/crawler and the tree does not compile, so I proved it directly in internal/tools, which builds standalone — encode-then-decode returns the input for both layers and reports no partial decompression. SEPARATE FINDING, filed as its own follow-up rather than buried here: Test_tools_encode_serves_every_encoding_the_ui_offers hard-codes seven encodings while its comment claims it reads ENCODE_ENCODINGS from data.workbench.ts. It does not, so the guarantee is fictional — offering 'brainfuck' leaves the suite green. Same shape as reference.ts's header promising a test that did not exist. A real extractor plus a decode-direction test is written and lands once the tree compiles.

title: wshistory: the frame table has no context menu — a frame cannot be copied, annotated or sent anywhere
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD by AuditProxy (Proxy-screen parity audit, 2026-08-27).

The WebSocket frame table has no context menu. A frame cannot be copied, sent
anywhere, commented or highlighted. The connection list beside it does have one,
which is what makes the omission look like an oversight rather than a decision.

## burpsy-side evidence

pages/wshistory.tsx:242-261 -- the frame VirtualTable is constructed with
ariaLabel, data, columns, getRowId, selectedId, onSelect, rowClassName, loading
and empty. No `menuGroups` prop is passed.

The same file DOES build a menu for the connection list:
  wshistory.tsx:171-197  menuFor(conn) -> MenuGroup[]
  wshistory.tsx:174      return actions.menu(exchangeDetail.data)
  wshistory.tsx:213      menuGroups={menuFor(conn)}
  wshistory.tsx:56       <ContextMenu groups={menuGroups}>{row}</ContextMenu>

and the page already imports the shared factory at wshistory.tsx:8
(`useExchangeActions`). So the mechanism is present in the file and simply not
applied to the frame rows.

Compare the two other HTTP tables, which do pass it:
  pages/history.tsx  menuGroups on the exchange table
  pages/intercept.tsx:728  menuGroups on the held-message table

## Burp-side evidence

Burp's WebSockets history is a first-class message table with the universal
context menu on its rows -- section 5.1 of
/root/burp-re/BURP_SUITE_UI_UX_SPECIFICATION.md states the send-to matrix is
invoked "on any HTTP Message editor or History table row", and the WS message
table carries per-message annotation (comment and highlight) the same way the
HTTP history table does.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Copy a frame's payload, annotate the one interesting frame out of thousands, or
send a frame anywhere. The frame is selectable and readable and that is all --
on a socket carrying application messages, the operator can find a frame only by
scrolling and can then do nothing with it but read it.

## Not a duplicate of burpsy-react-ui-5k4

5k4 is the missing FILTER surface on this page (how to find a frame). This is the
missing ACTIONS on a frame once found. Both are needed and neither closes the
other.

## Note

Comment and highlight on a frame need somewhere to store them: the annotation
route today is per-exchange (useAnnotateExchange, used at pages/history.tsx:424),
and a frame is not an exchange. Copy-payload and the send-to entries need no new
storage and are the cheap half.
acceptance_criteria: A WebSocket frame row offers a context menu with at least copy-payload and the send-to targets that apply to a frame; if comment/highlight are included, per-frame annotation is persisted rather than dropped.
close_reason: 63e101b8164900cbcd08697a60c61cda3dcab2d5. pages/wshistory.tsx now passes menuGroups={menuForFrame} to the frame VirtualTable. Payload group (copy payload as text or hex, send payload to Decoder / Comparer A / Comparer B, save payload to file) plus a frame group (copy frame id, copy frame summary line, show the connection's exchange in HTTP history). The payload entries appear once the per-frame fetch has returned and are withheld until then, with the group title saying so - the same discipline menuFor(conn) beside it already uses, and better than a Copy that silently copies nothing, since WsRow carries no payload and the bytes come from a separate fetch. Comment and highlight are deliberately NOT included, per the acceptance criteria's conditional: /api/ws/message/ is registered GET-only (internal/web/api_ws.go:184) and a frame has no notes/highlight field on the wire, so there is nowhere to persist them. That is stated in the code comment and is the one piece still needing backend work - a follow-up should add the fields plus a PATCH before the menu entries appear. tsc --noEmit clean.

title: proxy: out-of-scope traffic is always written to history — there is no 'don't log out-of-scope items' switch
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD by AuditProxy (Proxy-screen parity audit, 2026-08-27).

Scope narrows what burpsy DISPLAYS but never what it RETAINS. Every byte the
proxy sees is stored regardless of scope, and there is no switch to change that.

## Burp-side evidence

  BurpClass9621.java:68  "don't send items to proxy history or live tasks"
  BurpClass9621.java:69  "don't send items to live tasks"
  control name: configPanelProxyMiscellaneousDontLogOutOfScopeItems

  BurpClass9646.java -- configPanelProxyHistoryLogging (:35), title "Proxy
  history logging" (:40), described at :45 as choosing "whether Proxy
  automatically stops sending out-of-scope items to the history and other tools
  when you add an item to the Target scope", with three options:
  :78 "Stop logging out-of-scope items", :87 "Ask me what to do each time",
  :95 "Do nothing".

A dependent control also exists: TLS pass-through's "Apply to out-of-scope
items" (BurpClass9055.java:107), whose own tooltip at :108 states it
'Requires "Don't send items to Proxy history or live tasks, if out of scope" to
be enabled.' -- so in Burp this switch gates another feature.

## burpsy-side evidence

`grep -rniE "DontLog|dont_log|log_out_of_scope|LogOutOfScope" --include=*.go
--include=*.tsx internal/proxy internal/web/ui/src` returns ZERO.
Positive control, same invocation and same directories: the sibling alternation
patterns in that same grep DID return hits (keep-alive matched
internal/proxy/proxy.go:736-739; unpack matched internal/proxy/ws.go:801), and
`grep -ciE "listen" internal/proxy/proxy.go` -> 11. So the absence is real.

Not in internal/proxy/options.go:43-62 (complete OptionKeys enumeration).

Also absent, and part of the same Burp panel: "Automatically add entries on
client TLS negotiation failure" (BurpClass9055.java:98) is not in
pages/settings.tsx:395-484 (TlsPassthroughSection), which offers add and remove
of host patterns only.

burpsy states the retention/rewrite split deliberately at
internal/proxy/proxy.go:1658 -- "Scope decides what is *retained*, never what is
*rewritten*" -- but the retention switch itself is not exposed anywhere, so the
first half of that sentence has no control behind it.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Keep a capture confined to the target. On a long engagement against a scoped
host, reached through a browser that is also doing ordinary traffic, every
unrelated request is written to the store; the operator can hide it from the
table but cannot stop it being recorded, and the on-disk store grows with
traffic they are not authorised to retain.

## Note

Retention is the sharper edge of this than tidiness: an engagement whose rules of
engagement forbid capturing third-party traffic currently has no technical
control to honour that, only a display filter.
acceptance_criteria: An operator switch stops out-of-scope exchanges being recorded to the store (not merely hidden from the table); the switch is honoured by both the plaintext and TLS relay paths; the count of exchanges dropped for being out of scope is visible so an empty history is distinguishable from a mis-set scope.

title: session: rules have no tools scope, so a rule cannot be restricted to specific tools
description:
## Claim
Session rules are scoped by host only — there is no tools scope, so a rule cannot be restricted to some tools and not others.

## Burp-side evidence
`settings/sessions/session-handling-rules.html` — the rule editor's Scope tab has three axes:
> "**Tools scope** — The Tools scope settings are on the Scope tab of the session handling rule editor. These settings enable you to specify the Burp tools that each rule should apply to. Burp only processes rules for requests made by in-scope tools."
> "**URL scope** …"
> (and a **Parameter scope**, referenced by the note on "Replace matching part of the request": "it doesn't take into account the Parameter scope setting in the Scope tab")

`settings/sessions/index.html` shows why it is load-bearing rather than cosmetic:
> "There is a default session handling rule that updates requests made by the Scanner with cookies from Burp's cookie jar. This rule does not apply when the Scanner is managing its own sessions during crawling and crawl-driven auditing. You can disable this rule if required."

i.e. Burp's own shipped default rule is defined by its tools scope.

## burpsy-side evidence
The rule's only scope field is a host list — `internal/session/session.go:697`:
```go
ScopeHosts  []string  `json:"scope_hosts"`
```
consumed by `MatchHost` (`internal/session/session.go:717`), which is the whole matching predicate; `Coordinator.MatchingRule(host)` (`session.go:942`) takes a host and nothing else.

The editor is explicit that host is all that is read — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/session.tsx:49`:
> `/** Only host patterns are read server-side; an empty list means "applies everywhere". */`

and the flattening confirms it, `pages/session.tsx:113`:
```ts
hosts: (rule.scope?.rules ?? []).map((entry) => entry.host ?? "").filter(Boolean),
```
The wire scope document has an `allow_all` flag and `{kind, host}` rules (`pages/session.tsx:145`) — richer than the host list, but still only hosts.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## Related but separate
URL scope and parameter scope are the other two axes of the same tab. They are not claimed here because host scope is a partial substitute for URL scope (coarser, but the same axis), whereas tools scope has no substitute at all — there is no way to express it. Parameter scope only becomes meaningful once rules have parameter-setting actions, which is the separate rule-actions issue.

## What an operator cannot do
Keep a re-login rule away from a tool it would corrupt. Concretely: a rule that re-logs-in on a 302 will fire during an Intruder attack that is deliberately fuzzing the session cookie, and there is no way to say "this rule applies to Repeater and Scanner but not Intruder".
acceptance_criteria: A rule carries a set of tools it applies to, defaulting to all; the coordinator's rule-matching consults the requesting tool alongside the host, and a request from an out-of-scope tool does not trigger the rule. Covered by a test that fires the same request as two different tools and gets different behaviour.

title: session: a rule can only replay a macro on invalid session — 8 of Burp's 9 rule actions are unrepresentable
description:
## Claim
A session-handling rule can express exactly one action — replay the macro when the session is invalid — so eight of Burp's nine rule actions are unrepresentable.

## Burp-side evidence
`settings/sessions/session-handling-rules.html`, "Rule actions":
> "Click Add to add the following actions to your rules:
> - Add cookies from the session handling cookie jar.
> - Set a specific cookie or parameter value.
> - Check whether the current session is valid, and perform sub-actions conditionally on the result.
> - Prompt the user for in-browser session recovery.
> - Run a macro.
> - Run a post-request macro — this issues the current request, and then executes a further macro.
> - Invoke a Burp extension.
> - Set a specific header value.
> - Replace matching part of the request"

And the composition model: "Each rule includes one or more actions that should be carried out when the rule is applied. Burp performs these actions in sequence, unless one of the actions specifies that no further actions should be applied to the request."

## burpsy-side evidence
The rule struct has no action list — `internal/session/session.go:693-703`:
```go
type SessionRule struct {
    ...
    ScopeHosts  []string
    Steps       []MacroStep
    MaxAttempts int
    Validity    ...
}
```
The behaviour is hardcoded: check validity, and if invalid replay `Steps` up to `MaxAttempts` times (`internal/session/recovery.go`). That is Burp's actions 3 and 5 fused into the only thing a rule can be.

The editor matches — `internal/web/ui/src/pages/session.tsx` offers Name, Enabled, Max attempts (`:740-772`), scope hosts (`:774-823`), the validity check (`:825-879`), and macro steps (`:881-918`). No action list, no action ordering, no "stop processing further rules".

## Partial coverage elsewhere in the tree (checked, not assumed)
Two of the nine exist as standalone tools rather than rule actions:
- "Replace matching part of the request" and "Set a specific header value" are approximately `internal/matchreplace/` with the `pages/matchreplace.tsx` surface.

That coverage is real but not equivalent: match-and-replace rules are global, not scoped per session rule, not ordered against the other actions, and not conditional on a validity check. So the gap stands, and the estimate should account for the overlap rather than duplicating the engine.

"Add cookies from the cookie jar" is currently implicit and per-call-site rather than a rule action — filed separately (see the Repeater-only `cookieHeaderFor` issue).

## Decision needed before code
This is a data-model change, not an increment. Options:
1. Full action list on the rule — `Actions []Action` with a sum type, executed in order, honouring a stop flag. Matches Burp, and makes the existing validity+macro behaviour one composite action rather than the rule's identity. Largest change; everything else composes afterwards.
2. Add the two or three actions with the clearest standalone value (set cookie/param value, set header value, add cookies from jar) as optional fields on the existing rule shape. Cheaper, but locks in a shape that cannot express ordering, and each further action makes it worse.
3. Decline the extension actions permanently (there is no Burp-extension host to invoke) and the in-browser recovery prompt (no browser to drive), and scope the issue to the remaining six.

(3) should be settled first regardless of which of (1)/(2) is chosen, because it changes the count this issue is measured against.

## Classification
CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do
Handle a CSRF-token application. The canonical Burp recipe — run a macro to fetch a token, then set that token as a named parameter on the outgoing request — needs "run a macro" *and* "set a specific parameter value" in one rule, and the second half does not exist.
acceptance_criteria: A rule holds an ordered list of actions; at minimum "add cookies from the jar", "set a specific cookie or parameter value", "set a specific header value" and the existing validity-check-plus-macro are all expressible in one rule and execute in the stated order. Actions declined as out of scope (extension invocation, in-browser recovery prompt) are recorded as declined with the reason.

title: proxy: gzip/deflate HTTP messages cannot be unpacked, so compressed responses are unreadable in history and unreachable by every modification rule
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD by AuditProxy (Proxy-screen parity audit, 2026-08-27).

burpsy cannot decompress a gzip or deflate HTTP message. A compressed response
is unreadable in history and untouched by every response modification rule.

## Burp-side evidence

Burp's Proxy -> Miscellaneous panel (configPanelProxyMiscellaneous,
BurpClass9621.java) carries two checkboxes, declared as controls
proxyOptionsUnpackCompressedRequests and proxyOptionsUnpackCompressedResponses
(/root/burp-re/out/ui_report/setname_inventory.tsv), with the panel's
search-keyword set naming them at BurpClass9621.java:64-65 ("unpack gzip",
"unpack deflate").

## burpsy-side evidence

Not in internal/proxy/options.go:43-62, which is the complete OptionKeys
enumeration (six keys, none of them an unpack option).

The consequence is stated in burpsy's own panel copy at
pages/proxysettings.tsx:49:
  "Ask the origin for plaintext: with no decompressor on the proxy path,
   compressed responses are exactly the ones these rules cannot rewrite."

And the skip is counted rather than hidden -- Counters.SkippedCompressed
(internal/proxy/options.go:120), surfaced as the "Skipped: compressed" metric at
pages/proxysettings.tsx:108.

The only inflate anywhere in the tree is WebSocket-only and view-only:
internal/proxy/ws.go:801-811 (wsInflateForView), plus
internal/core/websocket_deflate.go. Nothing on the HTTP path.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP, honestly disclosed. Filed because the disclosure explains the
limitation rather than declining the feature -- it names the missing
decompressor as the cause, which is a gap statement, not a decision.

## What an operator cannot do

Read a gzipped response body in history, or have any response modification rule
apply to one. The only workaround burpsy offers is strip_accept_encoding, which
changes what the operator asks the origin for and is detectable server-side --
so the operator must choose between reading the traffic and observing the
traffic the client would really have received.

## Note on scope vs burpsy-react-ui-6s2

6s2 covers Burp's Miscellaneous panel generically ("strip comments, remove
unsupported encodings") and is P3. This is the one member of that panel that is
a real engine capability rather than a switch -- it needs a decompressor on the
HTTP path first -- so it is tracked separately and should not be closed by
building the panel.
acceptance_criteria: Compressed request and response bodies can be unpacked on the proxy path under an operator switch; an unpacked response is readable in history and is eligible for the response modification rules; the Skipped: compressed counter falls to zero for traffic the switch covers.
close_reason: Fixed in 8654a1b - BOTH halves, not just decode-for-view. (1) internal/httputil/contentencoding.go: DecodeBody + Unpackable for gzip and deflate (zlib-wrapped per the HTTP spec, with a raw-deflate fallback tried only when the zlib HEADER is rejected, never mid-stream, since re-reading a corrupt zlib stream as raw produces plausible garbage). br/zstd have no stdlib decoder so Unpackable reports false and the caller counts a named skip. 64 MiB cap, reported as an error rather than truncating: a rule applied to half a body hands the client a document cut in the middle. (2) internal/proxy: unpack_compressed_requests and unpack_compressed_responses, mirroring Burp's proxyOptionsUnpackCompressed* checkboxes. Chunk framing comes off before the decompressor, Content-Encoding is dropped with the encoding, Content-Length follows the new body, and ApplyResponse no longer returns early when only the unpack switch is on - a response decompressed and matched by no rule is still readable now. Counters per the honest-counting rule: UnpackedResponses/UnpackedRequests count messages actually decompressed, and SkippedUnsupportedEncoding is the subset where unpacking was ON and the encoding could not be decoded anyway, because 'the switch is off' is fixable and 'no brotli decoder in this build' is not. (3) MessageView gains content_encoding/decoded/decode_error; the decode sits BESIDE text, never instead of it, so captured bytes stay the bytes on the wire. Mutation: restoring the old unconditional compressed skip fails TestAResponseRuleReachesAGzippedBodyWhenUnpackingIsOn and both TestUnpackingWorksOnDeflateAndOnChunkedFraming subtests; dropping the decoded rendering fails TestAGzippedResponseIsReadableInHistory and TestAChunkedGzippedResponseIsDecoded. options_applier_binding_test.go's fixture was extended (compressed pair added alongside plaintext), as its own failure message instructs, never weakened. UI half open: proxysettings.tsx should render the two switches and two counters, and its line 49 copy ('with no decompressor on the proxy path...') is no longer true; the message pane can render 'decoded'. SEPARATE DEFECT FOUND, not filed by me: MessageView.Text is a JSON string, so any body that is not valid UTF-8 - every gzip body - comes back with each invalid byte replaced by U+FFFD. The stored bytes are exact; the wire projection of them is lossy for binary and has been since MessageView existed. Documented in internal/web/message_decode_test.go around line 82.

comments.author: FixBackendTruth
comments.text:
SCOPE NOTE for the inventory (issue is closed/done, this is calibration).

CLOSE TO THE FILED SCOPE, and smaller than the audit's own hedging implied. The task instruction allowed for doing only the decode-for-view half if it proved large. It did not: both halves landed in one sitting. If an estimate for this was going to be wrong it would have been wrong on the high side.

Why it stayed small: internal/proxy/options.go already had every piece the proxy half needed. splitMessage, dechunk, rebuild (Content-Length fixing), headerValue, and the counter discipline all existed for the response-modification rules. The real work was 40 lines of Options.unpack plus a stdlib gzip/zlib/flate wrapper. rebuild needed one extra flag to drop Content-Encoding. Anyone estimating a 'decompress X on the proxy path' issue in this tree should look at options.go first — the framing machinery is done.

Two things worth knowing for related issues:

1. The 'decode for view' half is where the surprise was, and it is NOT fully fixed. MessageView.Text is a JSON string, so any body that is not valid UTF-8 — which every gzip body is — comes back with each invalid byte replaced by U+FFFD. The STORED bytes are exact; the wire projection of them is lossy for binary and has been since MessageView existed. I added content_encoding/decoded/decode_error alongside text, which makes compressed responses readable, but the raw pane still cannot faithfully show any binary body. That is a separate, older defect affecting images, protobuf and every non-text response, not just compressed ones. Documented at internal/web/message_decode_test.go:82. NOT FILED — recommend filing.

2. br and zstd are deliberately NOT decoded: no stdlib decoder, so adding either means adding a dependency. Unpackable() reports false and the caller counts SkippedUnsupportedEncoding, kept separate from SkippedCompressed precisely because 'the switch is off' is fixable by the operator and 'this build has no brotli decoder' is not. If brotli matters for real targets that is a distinct, dependency-shaped issue.

RELATIONSHIP TO burpsy-react-ui-6s2 unchanged: 6s2 is the rest of the Miscellaneous panel; this was its one compression member and is done.

REMAINING (UI, not mine): proxysettings.tsx should render the two new switches (unpack_compressed_requests, unpack_compressed_responses) and the two new counters (unpacked_responses, unpacked_requests, plus skipped_unsupported_encoding). Its line 49 copy — 'with no decompressor on the proxy path, compressed responses are exactly the ones these rules cannot rewrite' — is NOW FALSE and must change; that is the same class of stale-disclosure defect as the eip copy. The history/message pane can render 'decoded'.

title: match & replace: no request-parameter-name or parameter-value targets — 5 of Burp's 7 HTTP rule types
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD by AuditProxy (Proxy-screen parity audit, 2026-08-27).

Burp's Match & Replace rule-type dropdown has seven HTTP targets. burpsy has
five: both parameter-level targets are absent.

## Burp-side evidence

The rule-type enum constants, recovered from the decompiled tree
(`grep -rhoE "REQUEST_(FIRST_LINE|HEADER|BODY|PARAM_NAME|PARAM_VALUE)|RESPONSE_(HEADER|BODY)"`
over /root/burp-re/out/clean/renamed_final/, present in BurpClass9688.java and
BurpClass13799.java):

  REQUEST_FIRST_LINE   -> burpsy HAS (request_first_line)
  REQUEST_HEADER       -> burpsy HAS (request_header)
  REQUEST_BODY         -> burpsy HAS (request_body)
  REQUEST_PARAM_NAME   -> MISSING
  REQUEST_PARAM_VALUE  -> MISSING
  RESPONSE_HEADER      -> burpsy HAS (response_header)
  RESPONSE_BODY        -> burpsy HAS (response_body)

Burp's proxy match/replace panel is configPanelProxyHttpMatchAndReplaceRules
(BurpClass9054.java), with the WebSocket set at
configPanelProxyWsMatchAndReplaceRules (BurpClass9069.java).

## burpsy-side evidence

pages/matchreplace.tsx:18-26 -- the TARGETS array, seven entries: the five Burp
HTTP targets above plus websocket_to_server and websocket_to_client (which Burp
also has). Neither parameter target appears.

The comment at matchreplace.tsx:17 states the Go handler is the constraint:
"The targets the Go handler compiles. An unknown one is refused with a 400, not
silently accepted." -- so this is a backend capability gap, not a dropdown that
is merely missing options.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Rewrite a parameter by NAME across all traffic -- renaming `debug` to
`debug_disabled`, or replacing every value of `role` -- without hand-writing a
regex against the raw request line or body. A raw-bytes regex is not equivalent:
the same logical parameter is encoded differently in a query string, a
form-urlencoded body, a multipart part and a JSON body, so one regex either
misses cases or matches text that is not a parameter at all.

## Note

This needs a parameter model, which is the actual work: to target a param name
or value the engine must parse the request into parameters and re-serialise
after substitution, per encoding. burpsy already derives query parameters for
history's "Parameterized" filter (pathParts / queryCount, used at
pages/history.tsx:571-572), but that is query-string only and read-only, so it
is a starting point rather than the model.
acceptance_criteria: A Match & Replace rule can target a request parameter by name and by value; substitution round-trips correctly for query-string and form-urlencoded parameters at minimum, and any encoding the engine cannot parse is reported rather than silently skipped.
close_reason:
Backend half done; closing with the UI remainder filed as a fresh, narrower bead.

The engine now declares all of Burp's HTTP rule targets: internal/matchreplace/matchreplace.go:18-30 declares TargetRequestFirstLine, TargetRequestHeader, TargetRequestBody, TargetRequestParamName, TargetRequestParamValue, TargetResponseHeader, TargetResponseBody (+ WebSocket to server/client beyond Burp's HTTP set), each wired to its direction in targetsDir (lines 293-297). The API names them on the wire: internal/web/api_toolkit.go matchReplaceTargetName() emits request_param_name / request_param_value, and its doc comment records the old defect this closed — both param targets used to fall through to a 'request_body' default, making a GET-then-PUT round trip silently destroy param rules; the round-trip test in api_toolkit_test.go now asserts every declared Target round-trips.

Remaining (moved to new bead): the React UI does not offer the two param targets — internal/web/ui/src/pages/matchreplace.tsx:19-27 TARGETS list and internal/web/ui/src/lib/types.policy.ts:17-24 MatchReplaceTarget union have only the 5 HTTP + 2 WebSocket values, so an operator cannot select param targets without hand-crafting the JSON. Engine+API verified this session via the round-trip test; UI list is a dropdown edit.

title: ui: tool tabs never signal attention — a held intercepted request is invisible from every other tool
description:
## Claim
Tool tabs never signal that a tool needs attention. With Intercept on and a request held, nothing outside the Proxy page says so — in Burp the Proxy tab highlights, which is how an operator notices their browser has stalled.

## Burp-side evidence
- Spec section 1.1, point 2: every tool module *"expose[s] a `ToolFrameProvider` (returns the root tool UI container) and a **`ToolTabFlasher` (handles tab highlight/attention animations)**."*
- Spec sections 4.1-4.12 name a per-tool flasher for each tool: `dashboardToolTabFlasher`, `proxyToolTabFlasher`, `scannerToolTabFlasher`, `repeaterToolTabFlasher`, and so on — it is a shell-wide contract, not a Proxy special case.

## burpsy-side evidence
- `app.tsx:602-620` renders each tool tab as icon + label only. The only conditional is the active class (`:610`) and `aria-current` (`:611`). No count, badge, dot or animation class.
- No such styling exists: `grep -n 'tool-tab' burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/styles.css` returns layout, hover, active and two responsive rules only (lines 277, 290, 298, 319, 324, 2559, 2562, 2579, 2582, 3484) — nothing attention-shaped.
- The data is already in the shell: `app.tsx:146` `useEventStream()`, and `app.tsx:156-158` already reads `live`, `lastEventAt`, `eventCount` off the connection store.

## Classification
UX DIVERGENCE.

## What an operator cannot do
Notice that interception is holding traffic while they are on any other tool. Their browser hangs, and the only way to find out why is to navigate to Proxy -> Intercept and look. Same for a finished audit or a new finding.
acceptance_criteria: A tool tab carries a visible attention indicator when its tool needs the operator — at minimum a held-message count on Proxy — driven off the existing event stream and visible from every other tool.

title: ui: mod+O Send to Organizer appears in the shortcut list and Settings table but is bound nowhere
description:
## Claim
Send to Organizer is listed in the shortcut registry as a rebindable action bound to mod+O, is shown in the shortcut modal and the Settings hotkey table, and is installed nowhere. Pressing it does nothing (or opens the browser's Open dialog).

## Burp-side evidence
- `tools/organizer/index.html` (Burp bundled docs): *"Alternatively, you can use the default hotkey Ctrl + O"*.
- Spec section 5.2 lists Send to Organiser / `Ctrl + O` / scope "HTTP Message / Table Row".

## burpsy-side evidence
- Declared: `lib/shortcuts.ts:45-49` — `{ id: "send.organizer", group: "Send to", label: "Send the selected exchange to Organizer", defaultChord: "mod+o", rebindable: true, note: "Burp binds Ctrl+O here too" }`.
- Rendered as a real, editable row: `lib/shortcuts.ts:111` `REBINDABLE` filters on `rebindable`, consumed by the Settings table (`pages/settings.tsx:1266`) and the modal (`app.tsx:41-67`).
- Installed nowhere: `grep -rn 'useChord(' --include=*.tsx src/` -> app.tsx only, and none of its five ids is `send.organizer`. The five hardcoded page bindings are `mod+r`, `mod+i` (`pages/history.tsx:615,626`), `mod+f`, `alt+t` (`pages/intercept.tsx:455,465`), `mod+enter` (`pages/repeater.tsx:147`) — no `mod+o` among them. `grep -rn '"mod+o"' --include=*.tsx --include=*.ts src/` -> no hits; positive control `grep -rn '"mod+r"' src/` -> `pages/history.tsx:615`.
- The action itself exists and works from the menu: `lib/actions.ts:624-634` `addToOrganizer`, exposed at `lib/actions.ts:814`.

## Classification
