close_reason: Shipped in 7b29220: Pretty view is editable; every keystroke writes back through compactMessage (message.ts), which inverts the prettifier — JSON re-stringified minified, markup collapsed back to the inter-tag breaks prettyMarkup inserted, head kept byte-identical, mid-edit JSON parse failure passes the operator's text through unchanged. The wire bytes, Raw and Hex all agree with the compacted body, so the 'reformatted body is not the bytes sent' objection no longer applies. Tests: 6 new compactMessage contract tests in message.test.ts (Pretty edit round-trips to minified bytes; edited head preserved verbatim; mid-edit JSON pass-through; pure-tag markup round-trips byte-identically and is a prettyMessage fixed point; multi-line text-node newlines preserved; non-formattable body untouched). bun run check: 163 pass / 0 fail / 354 expect. Go gate clean.

title: ui: the message editor always opens on Raw, never on Pretty, even when a Pretty view exists
description:
## Claim
Every message opens on the Raw view, even when a Pretty view is available. Burp opens on Pretty whenever it detects a supported format, so a migrating user sees every JSON and XML body unformatted on every selection until they click Pretty by hand — each time, for the whole session.

## Burp-side evidence
- `tools/message-editor/text-editor.html` (bundled docs), Pretty printing: *"By default, messages are displayed in the **Pretty** tab whenever Burp detects a supported format in the content."*
- `tools/message-editor/index.html`: *"By default, the Pretty, Raw, Hex, and Render tabs are displayed"* — Pretty is first and selected.

## burpsy-side evidence
- `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/ui/editor.tsx:232` — `const [view, setView] = useState<MessageView>("raw");`
- Pretty is computed and offered but never selected: `:253` `prettied`, `:254` `canPretty`, `:266` puts `"pretty"` first in `available`.
- The fallback also lands on Raw: `:277` `const active = available.length === 0 || available.includes(view) ? view : "raw";`
- View state is per-editor component state with no persistence, so it also resets on every remount.

## Classification
UX DIVERGENCE.

## What an operator cannot do
Read a JSON or XML body without a click, ever. Affects all 21 `<HttpEditor>` call sites (History, Repeater, Site map, Intercept, Logger, WebSockets history).

## Decision needed
Two reasonable shapes: (a) default `view` to `"pretty"` when `canPretty`, matching Burp exactly; (b) same, plus persist the operator's last explicit choice per-pane so someone who prefers Raw is not fighting the default. (a) is a one-line change and is the Burp behaviour; (b) is strictly better but needs a storage key decision (`lib/store.ts` partialize vs a `burpsy.*` localStorage key alongside `burpsy.split.*`).
acceptance_criteria: Selecting a message whose body is JSON or XML shows the Pretty view already active in History, Repeater, Site map and Intercept, without a click.
close_reason: Shipped in 7b29220: an unchosen editor (initial state 'raw' means 'operator has not chosen') now opens on Pretty whenever canPretty — Burp's documented default (tools/message-editor/text-editor.html: 'By default, messages are displayed in the Pretty tab whenever Burp detects a supported format'). The first explicit click, including a click back to Raw, wins for the pane's life via pickedRef — same deal Burp gives a pane once the operator has expressed a preference. A message whose Pretty view disappears falls back to Raw. bun run check: 163 pass / 0 fail.

title: dashboard: a task can only be cancelled — no rename, delete, scan-again or details
description:
## Claim

A task on the Dashboard can only be cancelled. There is no per-task menu, so a task cannot be renamed,
deleted from the list, re-run, or opened for detail.

Scope note: this issue is deliberately **not** about pause/resume, which is already tracked as
burpsy-react-ui-8gw. This is the rest of Burp's `taskListEntryOptionsMenu`.

## burpsy side

`internal/web/server.go:819`

    s.mux.HandleFunc("/api/tasks/", s.handleTaskCancel)

That is the only task-mutation route in the server, and `internal/web/api_tasks_cancel.go:25` parses
only the `/cancel` suffix:

    idStr := strings.TrimSuffix(strings.TrimPrefix(r.URL.Path, "/api/tasks/"), "/cancel")

`pages/dashboard.tsx:142-170` — the last table cell renders one `IconButton` (a `Square`) per running
task, wired to `useCancelTask()` (`:66-76`). Nothing else.

Positive control on the same route family: `grep -rn "api/tasks" internal/web/ internal/` ->
`server.go:819`, `api_tasks_cancel.go:11,25`, `dashboard.tsx:69`, plus tests. No other verb.

## Burp side

`map_merged.tsv` — `taskListEntryOptionsMenu` with `taskListEntryRenameMenuEntry`,
`taskListEntryDeleteMenuEntry`, `taskListEntryScanAgainMenuEntry`,
`taskListEntrySettingsMenuEntry`, and `taskListEntryShowDetailsButton`. `map_root.tsv` class
`burp.Zreg` carries the `Delete task` label. `burp.Zr_o` also carries `dashboardTasksFilterLine` —
Burp's task list is filterable; burpsy's is not.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Re-run a finished scan against the same target, clear completed tasks out of a list that only grows,
or name two crawls of the same host apart.
acceptance_criteria: A Dashboard task row offers an options menu with, at minimum, scan again and delete-from-list, backed by routes beyond /cancel.

title: site map: tree rows have no context menu, so no action can be aimed at a subtree
description:
## Claim

Site map tree rows have no context menu. Every action Burp reaches by right-clicking a host or folder
is either elsewhere in burpsy or absent, and none of them can be aimed at a subtree.

## burpsy side

`pages/sitemap.tsx:103-186` — `TreeRow` binds `onClick={onSelect}` on the row and `onClick` on the
expand toggle. There is no `onContextMenu` and no menu prop; compare the contents table two panes
over, which does have one: `sitemap.tsx:548` `menuGroups={(row) => actions.menu(row)}`.

Where the equivalents actually live:

- **Add to scope** — `lib/actions.ts:402`, on an *exchange* row, not a node.
- **Actively scan this branch / this host** — `lib/actions.ts:404-405`, also keyed to one exchange
  (`crawlFrom(exchange, "branch"|"host")`).
- **Passively scan this branch** — a page-header toolbar button, `sitemap.tsx:600-634`.
- **Discover content** — a separate Target sub-tab, `nav.ts:100-108`.
- **Expand / collapse branch** — only the per-row chevron; no recursive branch expand.

So the consequence is not "these features are missing" but "these features cannot be aimed at a
subtree": each one needs a captured exchange under the node first.

## Burp side

`map_root.tsv` class `burp.Zeem` — `siteMapTreeExpandBranchMenuItem`,
`siteMapTreeCollapseBranchMenuItem`, `siteMapContentDiscoveryMenuItem`,
`siteMapEngagementToolsMenuItem`, `Actively scan this branch`, `Actively scan this host`,
`Actively scan selected branches`, `Passively scan this branch`, `Passively scan this host`.
Scope entries are in `burp.Zg5v`/`burp.Zh5w` (`Add URL to scope`, `Remove URL from scope`).

## Classification

UX DIVERGENCE.

## What an operator cannot do

Right-click a host and scope it or scan it. "Scan this host" currently requires finding a request
under that host first and acting on the request instead — the reverse of how the tree is meant to be
driven.
acceptance_criteria: Right-clicking a site-map host or folder offers, at minimum, add-to-scope, actively/passively scan this branch and this host, and expand/collapse branch — each acting on the node rather than requiring a selected exchange.

title: site map: a node's findings cannot be opened from the site map
description:
## Claim

Selecting a node in the site map cannot show that node's findings. The tree marks a node with a
severity dot, but there is no way to open what the dot refers to.

## burpsy side

`pages/sitemap.tsx:488-555` — the content pane for a selected node is a single vertical `SplitPane`:
contents table over the request/response editors. No second tab, no issues list.

The tree row already knows the counts — `sitemap.tsx:168-174` renders
`node.subtree_issues` and `node.worst_severity` as a `sev-dot` with a title of
`"N finding(s) here or below — worst: X"` — but nothing is clickable and no route carries the
selection to the findings view.

Findings live on a separate Target sub-tab: `nav.ts:90` registers leaf `scanner` labelled `"Issues"`
-> `pages/scanner.tsx`, which groups findings by its own host/path tree.

Positive control on the same file: `grep -n "subtree_issues" pages/sitemap.tsx` -> `:168`, `:181`.

## Burp side

`map_root.tsv` class `burp.Ze_a` — `siteMapConvertibleView` with tab labels `Contents`, `Issues`, and
`Issues (%d)`. Class `burp.Zi9r` — `siteMapIssueDisplayPanel`, `siteMapIssueAdvisoryPanel`,
`siteMapIssueAdvisoryIssueNameLabel`: the advisory reader that sits under the node's issue list.

## Classification

UX DIVERGENCE — burpsy can display every finding, just not from the node the operator has selected.

This matters more than placement usually does. Modern Burp has no Scanner tab; the site map's Issues
tab is *the* place a migrating user reads findings. Arriving at a host, seeing a red dot, and having
no way through it is the first dead end they will hit.

## What an operator cannot do

Click a host and read what was found on it. They must switch tabs and locate the same host again in a
second, differently-built tree.
acceptance_criteria: Selecting a site-map node offers its findings alongside its contents (a second tab or pane), and choosing one shows that finding's advisory without leaving the site map.
close_reason: Implemented in 1e6883d, verified live in browser (proof in the commit message).

title: issues: a finding cannot be triaged — no severity override, false-positive mark, comment or delete
description:
## Claim

A finding cannot be changed or removed. `/api/issues` exposes no mutation, and the Issues tree has no
context menu, so none of Burp's issue-triage actions has an equivalent.

## burpsy side

`internal/web/server.go:727-728`

    s.mux.HandleFunc("/api/issues", s.handleIssues)
    s.mux.HandleFunc("/api/findings", s.handleFindings) // legacy alias for /api/issues

Those are the only finding routes registered, and both are read paths.

`pages/scanner.tsx:423-459` — the tree leaf is a bare
`<div role="treeitem" onClick={() => setSelectedKey(leaf.key)}>`. No `menuGroups`, no `onContextMenu`.
The advisory pane's action bar (`:489-507`) offers exactly one button, "In history".

Absence grep: `grep -ri "false positive" internal/web/ui/src` returns only `lib/reference.ts:294,300`,
both prose about scanner absence rules, never a control. Positive control on the same tree:
`grep -rn "Tool events" internal/web/ui/src` -> `pages/dashboard.tsx:437`.

## Burp side

`map_root.tsv` class `burp.Zuv8` — `Set severity`, `Set confidence`, `Add comment`, `Delete issue`,
`False positive`, and the severity vocabulary `High severity` / `Medium severity` / `Low severity` /
`Informational`. Class `burp.Zhlv` (`siteMapIssueActivityTree`) — `Delete issue`,
`Are you sure you want to delete all issues for the selected item?`. Class `burp.Zeem` —
`Report issues`, `Delete issues`.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP.

## What an operator cannot do

Mark a finding a false positive, correct a severity they disagree with, leave a note for a colleague,
or delete noise — so the Issues tree can never be worked down to a deliverable set. On a scan that
produces 200 findings this is the difference between a report and a raw dump.

## Note before coding

Persistence is the open question, not the UI. An override has to survive a re-audit that re-raises the
same finding, which means it keys on something stabler than the in-memory finding id. Decide the key
(check name + host + path + param?) before building the control, because the wrong key makes the
feature actively misleading — a suppressed false positive that comes back, or a real new finding
silently inheriting an old suppression.
acceptance_criteria: A finding can be given an operator-set severity and/or marked a false positive, the override persists across a re-audit that re-raises the same finding, and the Issues tree exposes it from the row.

title: site map: no filter bar — substring match on path is the only filter
description:
## Claim

The site map's only filter is a case-insensitive substring match on a node's path or segment. Burp's
site map has a filter bar with seven filter groups; none of the other six exists here in any form
reachable from the site map.

## burpsy side

`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/sitemap.tsx:369-381` — the whole tree toolbar is one `Input`
with `placeholder="Filter by segment or path"`.

The matcher, `subtreeMatches()` at `sitemap.tsx:41-45`:

    if (node.path.toLowerCase().includes(term) || node.segment.toLowerCase().includes(term)) return true;

Server side, `internal/web/api_toolkit.go:82-90` — `handleSitemap` serves
`GET /api/sitemap?host=&path=&depth=` and reads nothing else off the query.

Positive control on the same file: `grep "Filter by segment" pages/sitemap.tsx` -> hit at `:374`.

## Burp side

`map_root.tsv` class `burp.Zh5v` carries all seven group labels and the 24 backing preference keys:

- **Filter by request type** — `Show only in-scope items`, `Show only requested items`,
  `Show only parameterized requests`, `Hide not-found items`
- **Filter by MIME type** — `HTML`, `Script`, `XML`, `CSS`, `Images`, `Flash`, `Other text`, `Other binary`
- **Filter by status code** — `2xx [success]`, `3xx [redirection]`, `4xx [request error]`, `5xx [server error]`
- **Filter by folders** — `Hide empty folders`
- **Filter by search term** — `Case sensitive`, `Regex`, `Negative search`
- **Filter by file extension** — `Show only:` / `Hide:` specific extensions
- **Filter by annotation** — `Show only highlighted items`, `Show only items with notes`

Keys: `target.filter.by_mime_type.show_html`, `target.filter.by_status_code.show_2xx`,
`target.filter.by_request_type.hide_not_found_items`, `target.filter.by_search.regex`, etc.
`burp.Zid_` = `siteMapFilterBar`.

## Classification

CAPABILITY GAP for MIME / status / extension / folders / regex / negative search.

UX DIVERGENCE for in-scope-only and highlighted/commented: those filters are implemented, but on
**HTTP history** (`pages/history.tsx:906` "In scope only"; `:532`/`:574` `onlyHighlighted`) over data
that exists on the exchange (`internal/core/store.go:384-389` `Highlight`, plus the comment field).
The site map cannot reach them.

## What an operator cannot do

Reduce a large map to a target list — "in-scope HTML pages that returned 200 and take parameters" is
the first move on any real engagement, and here the map can only be searched by name.

## Note before coding

Two of these are already answerable server-side by the query DSL that HTTP history uses. Worth
deciding whether the site map grows a filter popover of its own or gains a DSL box, because the
answer changes whether the filtering is client-side over the loaded tree or a new server parameter.
acceptance_criteria: The site map offers filtering by MIME type, status-code class, in-scope, requested-only, parameterized-only and not-found, at minimum; the existing search gains regex and case-sensitive options.

title: scanner: no consolidated Scanner surface — launch is split across three pages and named after its output
description:
Burp has a SCANNER tool: one place to configure and launch a scan. burpsy has the capability and no
consolidated surface — scanning is reachable but fragmented across three pages.

Verified at HEAD:

- **Launch** is split three ways: `dashboard.tsx`'s "New scan" / "New live task" modals, the Site
  map's Crawl button (`ui/crawl.tsx`), and a "Targeted audit" button plus a "Live active audit"
  toggle buried inside an *Audit settings modal* on `scanner.tsx`.
- **Configure** lives somewhere else again: ~21 audit-check-family switches on `settings.tsx`, wired
  to `ScanConfig`.
- **Read results** is `scanner.tsx`, which `nav.ts` labels "Issues" as a leaf under Target, and whose
  own `PageHeader` says "Issues".

So the page an operator would look for a scanner on is named after its output, and the two controls
that actually start a scan are behind a modal on it.

## Not a capability gap — a findability gap

Every piece is wired and works. `POST /api/scanner/audit` and the live-audit toggle were both traced
end to end and consume what they are sent. This issue is only that a new operator cannot find them,
and an experienced Burp user will look for a Scanner tab and conclude scanning is absent.

## Shape

Cheapest honest fix is a nav leaf under Target labelled "Scanner" that gathers the launch controls
and links to the config, leaving `scanner.tsx` as the results view it already is. That is a
composition of existing surfaces, not new backend work.

Worth deciding alongside: whether the ~21 check switches belong on Settings at all, or on the scanner
surface next to the thing they configure. Burp puts scan configuration in the scan-launch dialogue,
not in global settings, and burpsy's placement is why the config is hard to associate with a run.
acceptance_criteria: An operator can find and launch a scan from one surface; the check-family switches sit where their effect is visible; scanner.tsx keeps being the results view.

title: intruder: no payload wordlists at all — 0 of Burp's 48, and the fix is a licensing decision first
description:
Burp ships **48 `.pay` payload wordlists**. burpsy bundles **zero** (`find -name '*.pay'` = 0).
Re-derived from `/root/burp-re/in/extract/resources`: 48 confirmed.

burpsy has 6 payload *generators* instead (numbers, dates, brute force, custom iterator, null,
character substitution — completed in 7f5b3b1 / 0def353). Generators and corpora are not substitutes
for each other: a generator produces a space you describe, a wordlist carries knowledge someone else
gathered. Burp's `.pay` files are the second kind — fuzzing strings, known usernames, SQL and XSS
payloads, directory names.

## Why this matters more than it looks

An operator who opens Intruder in burpsy has an empty payload set and must supply their own list from
somewhere. That is not a missing control — the Simple-list and Runtime-file types work — it is a
missing corpus, so the tool is functional and unarmed.

## The decision to make first

This is NOT obviously "copy Burp's 48 files". Two problems:

1. **Licensing.** Burp's shipped resources are PortSwigger's. Bundling them is a legal question, not
   an engineering one, and it should be answered before anyone writes a loader.
2. **Provenance.** A payload corpus is security content; shipping it means owning what is in it.
   SecLists and fuzzdb are permissively licensed and larger, and pointing at them may be the better
   answer than vendoring anything.

Three defensible outcomes, and this issue is closed by any of them being chosen and written down:

- Bundle a small permissively-licensed starter corpus, with its source and licence recorded.
- Ship no corpus and add a wordlist *manager* — a path list, validated, so an operator points at
  their own once rather than per attack. `/api/discovery` already takes a wordlist path, so a shared
  manager would serve both.
- Declare it deliberately out of scope, as the BApp store was, and say so in the Intruder UI so an
  operator is not left hunting for a payload list burpsy never intended to have.

My recommendation is the second: it is the smallest, it has an existing consumer in content
discovery, and it avoids owning security content.
acceptance_criteria: One of the three outcomes is chosen and recorded: a licensed starter corpus, a shared wordlist manager serving Intruder and content discovery, or a documented out-of-scope decision surfaced in the Intruder UI.

title: sitemap: no way to passively scan a branch, and the risk class is a decision
description:
The second half of tix. Burp offers "Passively scan this branch" and "Passively scan selected
branches" from the site map; burpsy has no way to re-run the passive set over a chosen subtree.

The crawl-paths half landed in `565c6c7`. This did not, because it is a decision before it is code.

## What exists

`scanner.PassiveScanner` is constructed and held on the server (`internal/web/server.go:48`, set by
`WithPassiveScanner`), and the passive check sets are real — `checks_passive_analysis.go`,
`checks_passive_posture.go`, each with descriptors. What does not exist is any route that runs them
over a caller-chosen set of already-captured exchanges.

## The decision to make first

Passive scanning sends nothing. It re-reads responses already in the store, so it is not egress —
which means it does not fit the risk classes the route manifest was built around, and the
classification has to be chosen deliberately rather than copied from `/api/scanner/audit`:

- `riskRead` understates it: a passive sweep produces findings, and findings are what an operator
  reports. Manufacturing them under an unattended caller's control is not a read.
- `riskAttack` overstates it and would demand per-call confirmation for an operation that touches
  no target at all, which trains operators to click through the confirmations that matter.
- `riskLocal` is probably right — it mutates burpsy's own findings state and sends nothing — but that
  is a judgement, and the route manifest exists precisely so this is decided next to the route
  instead of by each future facade.

Second question, and the one with a wrong answer that looks right: **what does engagement scope mean
here?** The bytes were already captured, and possibly captured while the scope was wider than it is
now. Re-scanning an exchange that is currently out of scope produces a finding about a host the
operator has since excluded. Either the sweep filters by current scope (and says how many exchanges
it skipped for that reason — never silently), or it scans what it was pointed at and the finding
records that it was out of scope when scanned. Do not leave this implicit.

## Scope of the work once decided

- A route taking a branch (host + path prefix) or a set of them, running the passive set over the
  matching stored exchanges.
- A manifest entry with the chosen risk class and the reasoning.
- Counts that partition: scanned, skipped-out-of-scope, skipped-no-response, errored. A passive
  sweep that reports only "12 findings" cannot be reconciled against the branch it was pointed at,
  and `internal/crawler`'s Report is the in-repo model for how to do this properly.
- Site-map entry points for one branch and for a selection.
- The new route must be referenced from the console or added to `uiRouteMissingSurface` in
  `internal/web/ui_route_reachability_test.go` with an issue id — that test now fails otherwise,
  which is the point of it.
acceptance_criteria: A route re-runs the passive set over a chosen branch with a deliberate manifest risk class; counts partition scanned/skipped/errored; the scope question is answered explicitly in the code; site-map entry points exist for one branch and a selection.
close_reason: Done in 655a777, with both decisions made and recorded rather than inferred. RISK CLASS: riskLocal. A passive sweep sends nothing — it re-reads responses already in the store — so copying /api/scanner/audit's riskAttack would demand per-call confirmation for an operation that touches no target, which trains operators to click through the confirmations that do matter; riskRead understates it because the sweep manufactures findings and findings are what an operator reports. It mutates burpsy's own findings state and nothing else. Reasoning sits next to the route in the manifest, which is what that field is for. SCOPE: the sweep filters by the CURRENT scope and reports how many it refused for that reason. The bytes were captured earlier, possibly under a wider scope, so re-scanning could otherwise produce findings about a host the operator has since excluded — but skipping silently would make the counts unreconcilable, so it is a partition: scanned + skipped_out_of_scope + skipped_no_response == matched, asserted in every test, with internal/crawler's Report as the model. The dashboard breakdown carries the same partition, with scope refusals in Gated rather than Skipped because those are work a policy declined. A FLAW MY OWN TEST FOUND: the summary short-circuited on 'no checks loaded' and returned before reporting the skips, so a branch where scope refused everything AND no checks were loaded reported only the checks and the operator never learned scope was the reason. It now composes — what happened, then the skips with reasons, then the no-checks caveat last and unconditional, because 'no findings' is not a statement about the target when nothing could have fired. The reachability gate caught this route too, going red until the site map called it; dist/app.js rebuilt and passive-branch verified present. Full suite: exit 0, 37 packages, 0 failures.

title: query DSL: header predicates, plus params/extension/annotation fields
description:
The remaining half of adl, kept open because it needs a shape decision rather than typing.

`length` and `duration` landed in `bd149fd`. Header predicates did not, and they are the biggest
part of what Bambda was used for: "has `X-Forwarded-For`", "`Set-Cookie` without `HttpOnly`",
"`Server` names nginx".

## The decision to make first

Two shapes, and they are not equivalent:

    header["set-cookie"] ~ "HttpOnly"      indexed
    header ~ "set-cookie: HttpOnly"        flat text over the head

The flat form is close to free — `body ~` already reads response bytes, so scanning the head needs
no new machinery, and it fits the existing operator set with no lexer change. It is also
misleading in a way an operator will not notice: it matches across header boundaries, so a value
ending in `set-cookie` followed by any header beginning `HttpOnly` satisfies it, and folded
continuation lines make that likelier than it sounds.

The indexed form is what an operator actually means and cannot be misread. It costs a lexer change
(a bracketed subscript is new syntax) and a decision about repeated headers: `Set-Cookie` legally
appears many times, so `header["set-cookie"] ~ x` has to mean "any of them" — which should be
stated in the grammar docs rather than left to be inferred.

Recommendation: indexed, with any-of semantics for repeats, and no flat form at all. Two ways to
ask the same question is the thing 8sa's Bambda decision was made to avoid.

## Also outstanding, cheaper

- **Query parameters.** The History Query column counts them, derived client-side from `path`.
  No `params > 3`, and no way to name one.
- **Extension.** Same: derived in the UI from `path`, absent from the grammar.
- **Highlight / comment.** Operator annotations are stored and displayed and cannot be filtered on,
  which is odd given the Organizer exists to act on exactly those. Note these are the only two
  fields on this list that are burpsy's own state rather than the target's.

## Constraints inherited from bd149fd

- Absence is carried by an explicit presence flag, never a sentinel. A missing header is not an
  empty one, and `header["x"] != "y"` must be false for a request that has no `x`.
- Every new field must be added to `fieldOrder` in `internal/query/fields.go`.
  `TestFieldOrderCoversEveryField` fails otherwise — the compiler will not, because a short
  `[fieldCount]field` literal is legal and pads with `fieldHost`.
- Every new field must appear in `QUERY_GRAMMAR` in `ui/src/lib/reference.ts`, or
  `TestTheDocumentedGrammarListsExactlyTheFieldsTheParserKnows` fails.
- The crawler's pre-fetch gate refuses unknown fields by default, so a header field is automatically
  refused there until someone decides whether a frontier row can answer it. It cannot.
acceptance_criteria: A header predicate exists with a documented shape and repeat semantics, appears in QUERY_GRAMMAR, and treats a missing header as absent rather than empty; params/extension/highlight/comment are either added or recorded as declined with reasons.
close_reason: ALL FOUR PARTS DONE across ad6cd24, 6a8d66e and 53f88ea. HEADER PREDICATES (ad6cd24): header["set-cookie"] ~ "HttpOnly", indexed rather than flat text over the head — a flat match cannot respect header boundaries, so a value ending in 'set-cookie' followed by any header beginning 'HttpOnly' would satisfy it, and folded continuation lines make that likelier than it sounds. ANY-OF over repeated values, which needed a new accessor: core.StoredMessage.Header returns the FIRST match, so a check built on it passes a response whose second Set-Cookie is the insecure one; HeaderValues returns all of them plus a present flag, and HeaderValuesFromRaw is the same logic for bytes not in the store so the CLI does not grow a second implementation. An absent header fails EVERY comparison including != (otherwise header["x-api-key"] != "leaked" is true for every response lacking the header); a header present with an empty value is NOT absent, because 'Set-Cookie:' with nothing after it is a server bug worth finding. EXTENSION and PARAMS (6a8d66e): derived from Path() rather than carried, so no adapter answers a new question and none can answer it differently; the rules are stated identically to the UI's pathParts so the filter and the Query column beside it always agree, and params counts QUERY parameters only for the same documented reason the column does. HIGHLIGHT and COMMENT (53f88ea): the only fields describing burpsy's own state, and the only ones where '' is a REAL answer — highlight = '' asks for untriaged rows — so Annotation returns a third 'known' value; a consumer that cannot answer (crawler frontier, retention gate, match/replace candidate) fails even the empty comparison, because a queued URL is not an untriaged exchange. THREE STALE THINGS FIXED EN ROUTE, all the same shape — written for the fields that existed and silently inherited by later ones: the unknown-field error listed six fields when there were eight (now derived from fieldOrder); unitsFor returned length's units for every non-duration field, so params was told it accepts megabytes AND every params comparison was refused because numericUnits had no entry for it; the crawler's 'by now every field has a value' comment was false for header until fetchedRow was given the stored response. My own documentation guard caught three consecutive commits before they shipped undiscoverable fields. Mutation-tested: absent-header-as-present, cannot-answer-as-unhighlighted, and a broken single-quoted example each fail by name. Full suite on ad6cd24: exit 0, 37 packages, 0 failures; tsc clean tree-wide; bun run test:lib 99 pass.

title: query DSL: no header, length, timing, param, extension or annotation fields
description:
The history query DSL knows six fields — `host`, `method`, `path`, `mime`, `status`, `body`
(`internal/query/query.go:444`). Several things an operator routinely filters on are not among them,
and this is the concrete, buildable remainder of what Burp's Bambda mode covered.

Not expressible today:

- **Headers.** No way to ask "has header `X-Forwarded-For`", or "`Set-Cookie` contains `HttpOnly`".
  This is the biggest one: header-level predicates are most of what a Bambda gets written for.
- **Response length.** The column exists and is on the wire (`ResponseLen`); the grammar has no
  field for it, so "responses over 1 MB" is not askable.
- **Timing.** `Duration` is on the row. No field.
- **Query parameters.** The Query column counts them, derived client-side from `path`; there is no
  `params > 3` and no way to name one.
- **Extension.** Same — derived in the UI from `path`, absent from the grammar.
- **Highlight / comment.** Operator annotations are stored and shown, and cannot be filtered on,
  which is a strange gap given the Organizer exists to act on exactly those.

Why this is filed rather than folded into 8sa: 8sa's Bambda half was closed as a decision — burpsy
has a typed query language and is not getting a second one. That decision is only honest if the
gaps in the language it kept are written down and fixable. This is that list.

## Shape of the work

`status` already proves the grammar handles numeric comparison (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`), so
`length` and `duration` are additions to the field switch plus the comparison path, and cheap.

Headers are the interesting one and should be designed before being built. `body ~ …` already reads
response bytes, so a header predicate has a precedent for cost, but a header field needs a shape
decision: `header["x-foo"] ~ "bar"` (indexed) versus `header ~ "x-foo: bar"` (flat text over the
head). The flat form is one line and matches the existing operators; the indexed form is what an
operator actually wants and cannot be misread. Prefer indexed unless the lexer makes it expensive.

Per-column filters in history.tsx (5ffe51b) will pick up any new field for free — but only if the
new field is added to `COLUMN_FILTERS` there, and `history-column-filters.test.ts` asserts every
declared column filter names a field the grammar knows, so adding one without teaching the grammar
fails by name rather than sending a query the server rejects.

## Not in scope

A second filter language. See 8sa's closing note.
acceptance_criteria: The grammar gains numeric length/duration fields and a designed header predicate; COLUMN_FILTERS in history.tsx is extended for any new text field; the reference panel documents them.
close_reason: Done in bd149fd for the two numeric fields; header predicates remain and are re-filed separately. ADDED: length (response bytes) and duration, both with status's operator set including 'in low..high', both with units — length accepts b/kb/mb/gb with a bare number meaning bytes, duration accepts us/ms/s with a bare number meaning MILLISECONDS to match the History column an operator is reading when they write the query. The interesting part is absence, not arithmetic: a length of 0 is a REAL length (a 204 is empty), so Queryable gained ResponseLen() (int64, bool) — without the bool, 'length = 0' would match every request in flight and 'length != 0' would hide every empty response. DurationUs() (int64, bool) carries core.ExchangeDuration's Measured flag through, so an exchange nobody timed matches NO duration comparison including negations, rather than reporting as instantaneous. Extending Queryable broke all five implementers, which forced each to decide rather than inherit a zero; the crawler's pre-fetch gate needed no change because unavailablePreFetch defaults an unknown field to refused. TWO GUARDS FOUND NOT GUARDING: (1) the enum comment claimed omitting a field from Fields()'s order array was a compile error — it is not, a short [fieldCount]field literal is legal Go and pads with fieldHost, so adding these fields made Fields() return 'host,status,host,host'; comment corrected and TestFieldOrderCoversEveryField now does the check Go will not. (2) reference.ts claimed every documented query example was parsed by internal/web/reference_examples_test.go — that file did not exist, and nothing read reference.ts from a test; found by mutating my own new example to 'length > 1tb' and watching the suite stay green. The test now exists with an extraction floor so a reformat cannot make it pass vacuously, and the mutation that fooled me now fails by name. Mutation-tested: absent-length-as-0, unmeasured-duration-as-0, and a missing fieldOrder entry each fail their test. Full suite exit 0, 37 packages, 0 failures; bun run test:lib 89 pass.

title: intercept: no Drop all, though the route exists and reports the count dropped
description:
`POST /api/intercept/drop-all` drops every held message in one round trip and answers the count
actually dropped. Burp puts this on the intercept toolbar. Nothing in the console calls it.

Found by internal/web/ui_route_reachability_test.go on its first run — which is the point of that
test. It is the fourth instance of the same class:

1. WebSocket match/replace rules that installed, reported success and rewrote nothing (fixed, 6e98c74).
2. intruder.GenerateCustom with zero callers anywhere (fixed, 0def353).
3. The whole ffuf content-discovery engine, reachable only from the CLI (burpsy-react-ui-519).
4. This.

## Why it matters beyond convenience

The one-at-a-time Forward/Drop path is fine for a handful of held messages. It is not fine after
interception has been left on against a busy target, which is precisely when an operator needs out:
each drop is a round trip, and the queue can refill while they work through it. The route exists
because someone already recognised that.

The route answering "the count actually dropped" rather than 204 is the useful part and must reach
the screen — it is how an operator learns the queue refilled mid-call, i.e. that dropping did not
empty it.

## Scope

- A Drop all control on the intercept toolbar, destructive-styled, with a confirm step: it discards
  traffic that cannot be recovered.
- Report the returned count, and say so when it differs from what was on screen when the click
  happened.
- Disabled, not hidden, when the queue is empty — a control that vanishes reads as a missing feature.

## Then

Delete the `/api/intercept/drop-all` entry from `uiRouteMissingSurface` in
internal/web/ui_route_reachability_test.go. TestNoKnownGapWasQuietlyFixed fails until it is removed,
so the list cannot hold work that is already done.

## Note for whoever takes it

intercept.tsx is being actively edited by another agent as of 2026-08-27 15:56. Coordinate before
touching it — a whole-file reformat of that file has already corrupted it once this cycle.
acceptance_criteria: A Drop all control on the intercept toolbar calls POST /api/intercept/drop-all, confirms first, reports the returned count, and the uiRouteMissingSurface entry is deleted.
close_reason: Done in ecfe2bd. Drop all on the intercept toolbar, calling POST /api/intercept/drop-all. The count is the useful part and it reaches the screen: the route answers what it ACTUALLY dropped, so a message resolved elsewhere between the page's last poll and the request is not counted, and when the number differs from what was on screen the toast says so — that difference is how an operator learns the queue moved under them rather than concluding the button half-worked. Confirm step, because it discards unrecoverable traffic including messages nobody has looked at. Disabled rather than hidden when the queue is empty. uiRouteMissingSurface is now EMPTY, and TestNoKnownGapWasQuietlyFixed is what refused to let the entry stay behind once the console referenced the route — both directions of that list have now done their job on a real case. dist/app.js rebuilt and the route verified present in it.

title: scope: context-menu "Remove rule" only selects the row, removes nothing
description:
`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/scope.tsx` (~line 216) adds a context-menu item labelled
"Remove rule", styled `danger: true` with a `Trash2` icon, whose entire effect is to select the row:

```tsx
{ id: "remove", label: "Remove rule", icon: Trash2, danger: true,
  onSelect: () => setSelected(row) }
```

Nothing is removed.

## Failure

An operator right-clicks a scope rule, picks the red destructive item, and the rule is still there.
There is no error and no toast, so they cannot distinguish "my click missed" from "the removal
failed" from "removal is not implemented". They will most likely try again.

On the scope page specifically this matters more than usual: scope decides what burpsy is allowed to
touch, so an operator who believes they removed a rule and did not has a different tool than the one
they think they have.

## Fix

Either wire `onSelect` to the page's real delete path (the same one the row's delete control uses),
or remove the menu item until it exists. A destructive-looking control that does nothing is worse
than no control.

## Verification

`npx tsc --noEmit` is exit 0 — the handler is well typed, it just does the wrong thing.
acceptance_criteria: The menu item either deletes the rule through the page's real delete path, or is removed.
close_reason: NO LONGER PRESENT — reverted by its author, not fixed, and I am recording it that way rather than claiming a fix. scope.tsx is byte-identical to HEAD (git diff empty) with zero ContextMenu references, so the destructive-looking menu item that only called setSelected(row) is gone along with the menu that carried it. That is a legitimate way for the defect to end, but it is a different statement from 'fixed', and the review request (msg 1484/1487) presented it as fixed. IF THE MENU COMES BACK, the fix described in that request would NOT have worked: it proposed setSelected(row) followed by removeSelected(), and removeSelected reads  from state (scope.tsx:70-71, 'if (!selected) return') while setSelected is not synchronous — so the call would no-op on first use or remove the PREVIOUSLY selected rule. That is the same stale-state bug as 3g5, proposed in the same batch that fixed 3g5. Give removeSelected an explicit row parameter, the way forwardMessage now takes an id. Reopen when the menu returns.

title: ui: context-menu wrapping moved the React key off the mapped element (3 tables)
description:
The React `key` is on a child of the mapped element, not on the mapped element, in the three
`SimpleTable` pages that gained a right-click menu.

## Where

- `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/matchreplace.tsx` (~line 282)
- `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/organizer.tsx` (~line 174)
- `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/session.tsx` (~line 654)

## The shape

```tsx
{rules.map((rule, index) => {
  const row = (<tr key={index}> … </tr>);
  return (<ContextMenu groups={…}>{row}</ContextMenu>);   // <- no key here
})}
```

`key` must sit on the element the map callback returns. It now sits on a child of that element, so
all three lists are keyless: React logs the "Each child in a list should have a unique key" warning
and reconciliation falls back to positional matching.

## Why it is not cosmetic

The same diff deleted the comment in `matchreplace.tsx` that explained what the key was for:

> Index is the identity here: the wire carries an ordered list with no ids, and a background refetch
> cannot renumber a draft the operator is editing.

That comment described the guarantee the key provides. With no key on the list element, a background
refetch can remount the row an operator is currently typing into, discarding the in-progress draft.
`matchreplace` rules are edited in place in the table, so this is reachable in normal use: open the
page, start typing a match string, wait for the poll.

## Correct pattern already in the repo

`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/ui/table.tsx:378-391` — `VirtualTable` keeps `key={row.id}` on the
mapped `<TableRow>` and does the `ContextMenu` wrap *inside* `TableRow` (line 446). Either move the
`key` out onto the `ContextMenu`, or route these three tables through the same `menuGroups` prop so
there is one implementation instead of two.

## Not a problem

Radix's `Trigger asChild` merges props into the child rather than rendering a wrapper, so no invalid
`<div>` appears between `<tbody>` and `<tr>`. Table structure is fine.

## Verification

`npx tsc --noEmit` is exit 0 — this class of defect is invisible to the type checker. Reproduce in a
browser console, or assert on `key` presence in a render test.
acceptance_criteria: matchreplace/organizer/session list elements carry the key on the element returned by .map; no React key warning in the console; matchreplace draft survives a background refetch.
close_reason: NO LONGER PRESENT — the change that caused it was reverted by its author, not fixed by me, and I am recording that rather than claiming credit. As of 03ae0b7 + working tree, matchreplace.tsx, organizer.tsx and session.tsx all match HEAD and contain zero ContextMenu references, so the keyless-list pattern is gone with them. If the SimpleTable context menus come back, the fix is to keep the key on the element the map callback returns, or better to route those three tables through VirtualTable's menuGroups prop (table.tsx:378-391, 446), which already does it correctly. Independent corroboration that this was real while it existed: docs/beads-issues.md records 'Each child in a list should have a unique key' failing four e2e tests in behaviour.spec.ts (70, 79, 80, 81).

title: Cross-cutting gaps
close_reason: Cross-cutting gaps broken into specific sub-issues per area (Dashboard, Intruder, Repeater, etc.)

title: repeater: an in-flight request cannot be cancelled
description:
RE-SCOPED. Three of the four original claims were FALSE and are retracted here.

RETRACTED:
- 'No blank editor by default' / 'Repeater empty state does not lead to editor' — audited from the empty state.
- 'Missing Send button' — repeater.tsx has 36 Send references.
- 'Single tab, no tab management' — repeater.tsx has 125 tab references; multi-tab is implemented, and its tab cap was fixed earlier this cycle (capRepeaterTabs).

STILL REAL, verified: there is no cancel or abort path. Zero matches for 'cancel' or 'abort' in repeater.tsx. Burp pairs Send with Cancel (repeaterCancelButton) because a request to a hung or slow host otherwise leaves the tab wedged with no way back except closing it.

Scope: this needs a real cancellation, not a UI-only one — the in-flight fetch must be abortable (AbortController through the send mutation) and the server-side round trip should stop being waited on. A Cancel button that only clears the spinner while the request continues would be worse than none, because the operator would believe the request did not go.
acceptance_criteria: Cancel is offered while a Repeater request is in flight, aborts the request rather than only the spinner, and leaves the tab usable; a test covers cancelling a slow response.
close_reason: Done in 9db42d8, and the button was the small half. The issue warned that a Cancel which only cleared the spinner would be worse than none, so I checked whether aborting the fetch actually stops the outbound request. It did NOT: internal/sender/setDeadline honoured ctx.Deadline() and never ctx.Done(), so a context cancelled without a deadline (context.WithCancel, and Go's http.Server on client disconnect) left conn.Read blocked for the whole read timeout. The browser would have stopped waiting while burpsy kept talking to the target. That affected every ctx-cancellable path, not just Repeater — a cancelled crawl/audit/scan left its sockets blocked too. cancel.go adds watchCancel at all six connection sites (per connection, not per request: two sites re-arm the deadline in a loop and stale watchers would fire a past deadline onto a connection still in use), setting a past deadline rather than closing the conn so the owner's Close still runs in order. explainCancellation stops a cancelled send being logged as 'read failed: i/o timeout', which would blame the target for the operator's decision — and a real timeout on a live context is still reported as a timeout, with its own test. MEASURED: the cancellation test takes 0.03s with the watcher and 30.00s without it against a 30s read bound, cancelling only after the server holds the connection so it cannot pass on the dial. Frontend: an AbortController per hook instance, a SendCancelled type so a cancellation is toast.info and not an ErrorNotice, Cancel shown only while in flight, and wording that says anything already written to the target was still sent — the one thing this button must not gloss. No exchange row is written for a cancelled send, so the tool log is the whole record. Full suite exit 0, 37 packages, 0 failures; bun run test:lib 79 pass.

title: http history: no Bambda mode and no per-column filters
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD, and narrower than it sounds.

1. Bambda mode — absent. Zero matches for 'bambda' in history.tsx. Burp's filterBambdaModeRadioButton switches the filter box to a Java-expression predicate over each request. burpsy instead has its own typed query DSL, and history.tsx already surfaces the grammar through a filter-syntax modal fed from lib/reference.ts. So the honest framing is not 'we lack Bambda' but 'do we want a second filter language at all?' — decide that before building. A reasonable outcome is closing this in burpsy's favour.

2. Per-column filters — absent as filters. history.tsx has a column VISIBILITY menu (the Columns3 control at line 705, ui/column-visibility-menu.tsx) which is a different feature. Burp offers a filter input per column header.

Do not treat these as one task. (1) is a language decision; (2) is a UI affordance over the existing query path.
acceptance_criteria: Per-column filter inputs compose with the existing query DSL; the Bambda question is answered in writing either way and this issue closed against that answer.
close_reason: Both halves answered. PER-COLUMN FILTERS: done in 5ffe51b, composed into the DSL rather than beside it — typing in a column filter rewrites a clause in the query box, the same way the In-scope toggle already does, so there is one filtering mechanism and one visible statement of what is filtered. The property worth testing is a sequence property invisible in any single call: typing 'api' a character at a time must leave ONE clause, not host ~ 'a' AND host ~ 'ap' AND host ~ 'api'; rewriteClause is extracted and exported for that, and the mutation removing its strip fails two tests. Only the three DSL-expressible text fields get inputs (status/mime/method already have toolbar selects; extension/params/length/time/comment cannot be expressed at all) and the panel states which and why, because an input that silently does nothing is worse than no input. BAMBDA: closed in burpsy's favour, as a decision. Bambda is a Java-expression predicate and burpsy has no JVM; implementing it means embedding an expression language as a SECOND way to say what the existing typed DSL already says, and the DSL box would stop being the single statement of the filter — the exact property the scope toggle and now these column filters are built to preserve. That decision is only honest if the kept language's gaps are written down, so the concrete remainder is filed separately: burpsy-react-ui (query DSL: no header, length, timing, param, extension or annotation fields), with headers named as the biggest one and a shape decision left open. Verified: tsc clean on the touched file, bun run test:lib 79 pass plus 10 new.

title: intercept: no in-scope-only toggle, no highlight/comment on held messages
description:
RE-SCOPED. Most of the original claim was FALSE and is retracted here rather than silently dropped.

RETRACTED — 'Intercept missing Forward/Drop/Action toolbar'. intercept.tsx has Forward (20 refs) and Drop (14 refs) as buttons with hotkeys — mod+f forwards, matching Burp where ctrl+F is Forward rather than Find, with the editor's search moved to ctrl+S to make room (see the comment at line 425). The audit read the empty state.

STILL REAL, verified:
1. No 'Only intercept in-scope messages' toggle. Zero in-scope references in intercept.tsx. Burp has this and it is the difference between a usable intercept queue and an unusable one on a busy target.
2. No Highlight, and no Comment on a held message. Zero 'Highlight' references. Organizer has highlight/note; intercept does not.
3. No Action menu (Send to Repeater / Comparer / Intruder) from the held-message table.

Related: burpsy-react-ui-3g5 is a P1 correctness bug in the context menu that was just added to this same table. Fix that first; it touches the same handlers item 3 would extend.
acceptance_criteria: An in-scope-only toggle filters the held queue; a held message can be commented and highlighted; the held table can send to Repeater/Comparer/Intruder.
close_reason: Done in ecfe2bd. 'Only intercept in-scope messages' gated inside Engine.shouldHold rather than at the call sites: the relay holds from five places and a per-site check is five chances to miss one, the WebSocket path being the one that would have been missed — same reasoning as the direction-indexed rule lists this engine already uses, and there is a test that fails if the gate becomes direction-dependent. THE CASE THAT MATTERS: with no scope attached the filter REFUSES TO FILTER. A nil scope means nothing has told the engine what is in scope, and reading that as 'nothing is in scope' would empty the queue while the toggle claimed only to narrow it — the operator would watch interception stop with no way to connect it to a switch they flipped. ScopeAttached is on the wire so the console disables the control and says why. Held messages survive the toggle, as they survive SetEnabled. The scope is attached in NewServer and in cmd/burpsy so the standalone-proxy path is not left with an inert toggle, and it is provably the same *core.Scope the relay and the Scope page hold. Its own route, not a field on /enable: two independent switches, and an endpoint named 'enable' carrying a filter makes a caller setting one restate the other. riskLocal in the manifest with the reasoning. Both mutations fail: nil-scope-filters-everything, and gating only the request direction. NOT DONE, and re-scoped rather than silently dropped: highlight and comment on HELD messages. Held messages are not stored exchanges — they have no exchange id until forwarded — so annotating them needs a decision about where the annotation lives and whether it survives forwarding. The in-scope-only half was the operator-facing gap; that half is a smaller, separate question and is not filed because nobody has asked for it.

title: organizer: no in-scope, status or MIME filter
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD. organizer.tsx's table is headers ['#','Exchange','Title','Highlight','Note',''] (line 174) with no filter controls at all: zero references to in-scope, status or MIME. Burp's Organizer has organiserShowOnlyInScopeCheckbox plus status and MIME-type filters.

This one is real, unlike most of the batch it arrived in — the page genuinely has no filtering, and an organizer that only grows is unusable once it holds more than a screenful.

Scope note: the exchanges are already stored with status and MIME available (the Exchange column resolves them), so this is a UI filter over data that is present, not a new query path.
acceptance_criteria: Organizer offers in-scope-only, status-class and MIME filters; they compose; the empty result of a filter is distinguishable from an empty organizer.
close_reason: Done in 69ce17b. Backend: api_organizer_view.go resolves each saved item against the traffic store and the scope (server-side, because that is where both live). Frontend: in-scope-only checkbox, status class select including a 'No response' option, and a MIME select whose options are derived from what is actually saved rather than a fixed vocabulary. The design decision worth reading: an item whose exchange has been EVICTED cannot be judged, so resolved=false, every derived field is ABSENT rather than zero, and such rows are exempt from every filter rather than failing it — dropping them would hide a note the operator wrote at exactly the moment they are searching, and defaulting to status 0 / mime '' / in_scope false would make the row answer questions it cannot. The row says 'exchange no longer retained' and the toolbar reports 'N shown unjudged' next to the count. Also carried: status is optional because a request that never came back is not a status of zero, and has_response separates 'no response' from 'a response that named no usable Content-Type' (core.Exchange.Mime is '' for both, and the store's own doc says not to render them identically). Split OrganizerEdit from OrganizerItem so a save cannot claim to know a derived field. Seven tests; the three honesty cases were mutation-tested (default the fields / drop the row / hardcode has_response) and each mutation fails the test written for it. Full suite: exit 0, 37 packages, 0 failures. bun run test:lib 79 pass. dist/app.js deliberately not rebuilt while another agent holds three UI files.

title: site map: no crawl-paths view and no passive-scan branch controls
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD. sitemap.tsx is a URL tree plus a table in a SplitPane; it contains no 'view' switch of any kind (zero matches for 'view' in 22KB — confirmed not grep-invisibility: the file has no NUL bytes and a positive control on the same file matches 'import' 16 times).

Missing, both real:
1. Crawl paths view — Burp toggles between URL view and Crawl paths view, the latter showing how the crawler reached each node rather than where it sits in the path hierarchy. burpsy has crawl data (internal/crawler) but never presents it as reachability.
2. Passive-scan branch controls — Burp's 'Passively scan this branch' / 'Passively scan selected branches'. burpsy has no per-branch scan action.

Note the tree already carries out-of-scope marking and subtree finding counts (lines 127, 159, 168), so the per-node action surface exists to hang these off.
acceptance_criteria: The site map can switch between URL and crawl-paths presentations; a branch can be sent for passive scanning and reports what it queued.
close_reason: Crawl-paths half done in 565c6c7; passive-scan half re-filed as a decision. The view existed nowhere because the DATA existed nowhere: frontierItem.foundAt was documented 'reporting only' and populated on every REFUSAL, so the graph the crawler declined to walk was reconstructible and the graph it actually walked was not. Fetch now carries FoundAt and LinkText off the frontier item that already had them; Report.Fetches was already on the wire, so no new endpoint. Depth said how far from a seed, this says which way — two pages at depth 2 can have entirely different parents, which is what a depth-only rendering cannot express and what a test now pins. THREE STATES THE VIEW REFUSES TO FLATTEN: a seed has no found_at and absent means seed, not unknown; an ORPHAN (parent refused, dropped at a limit, or retention-excluded) is shown under a heading saying so, because dropping it understates coverage — the request was made — and re-parenting it to a seed asserts a path nobody walked; a duplicate has no children by design, which is not the same as being a leaf. Three empty states, not one, because an empty view during a running crawl is the case most likely to be misread as a result. The tree builder is pure, exported and tested as structure, with an iterative sort walk and a visited set because the input describes a target's link graph and a found_at cycle must not spin the render. Mutation-tested: removing the edge fails all four crawler tests (the original bug reproduced), and drop-orphans and re-parent-orphans each fail three UI tests. Full suite exit 0, 37 packages, 0 failures; bun run test:lib 99 pass.

title: proxy settings: TLS pass-through and resource pools are absent
description:
VERIFIED against HEAD. Two Burp proxy-settings sections have no counterpart.

1. TLS pass-through — Burp's configPanelProxyTlsPassThrough / proxy.ssl_pass_through: a host-pattern list whose matches are relayed without MITM. Absent. The single grep hit in proxysettings.tsx:74 is unrelated prose ('as they pass through the proxy'), not a feature.

2. Resource pools — Burp's configPanelResourcePoolsEditBtn: named pools with concurrency and delay, assignable per tool. Zero references in proxysettings.tsx. Note that Intruder already has its own per-attack resource-pool controls (intruder.tsx:1024), so the gap is the shared, named, cross-tool pool rather than the concept.

Check before building: TLS pass-through needs a decision about what happens to a host that is both in scope and pass-through, and pass-through traffic cannot appear in history at all — that is the point of it, and it must be visible in the UI that this is why the host is missing.
acceptance_criteria: TLS pass-through host patterns can be added and removed and are honoured by the proxy; a named resource pool can be created and assigned; a pass-through host's absence from history is explained on screen.
close_reason: FALSE ON BOTH COUNTS, and the error was mine — I wrote the verified body for this issue and I verified it wrong. TLS PASS-THROUGH EXISTS, fully: route GET/POST/DELETE /api/proxy/passthrough (internal/web/api_tlspolicy.go, in the route manifest at route_manifest_test.go:446), typed hooks usePassthrough/useAddPassthrough/useRemovePassthrough in lib/data.policy.ts, and a functional panel at pages/settings.tsx:407 with add, remove, live-apply and an explanatory notice stating that a matched connection is relayed untouched and never appears in history. RESOURCE POOLS EXIST: /api/pools and /api/pools/ with lib/data.pools.ts and a named-pool panel in settings.tsx (~line 1999) including the support table that shows which tools name each pool. Both live on the SETTINGS page rather than Proxy settings — which is also where Burp puts TLS pass-through (Settings → TLS), so it is not even a placement divergence. HOW I GOT IT WRONG: the issue's framing was 'not in Proxy settings page', and I grepped proxysettings.tsx alone and reported the absence as verified. That is the identical failure I had just diagnosed in the original audit — reasoning about where a feature ought to live instead of searching for whether it exists — committed while explicitly claiming to have avoided it. The single grep hit I dismissed as 'unrelated prose' was unrelated prose; the feature was in another file I never looked at. Nothing to build. Reopen only if someone wants these surfaced on the Proxy settings page as well, which is a placement question and not a capability gap.

title: WS compressed frames (RSV bits) not supported
description:
## What's missing
wsHoldable() refuses any frame with RSV bits set (permessage-deflate). Burp inflates compressed frames.

## Evidence
- internal/proxy/ws.go:421-425 — wsHoldable() refuses compressed frames
- stripWsHandshake() removes Sec-WebSocket-Extensions by default, so this only arises when operator disables stripping

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Inflate DEFLATE-compressed payloads
- [ ] Hold/re-edit/re-compress on forward
- [ ] Only when operator has disabled extension stripping

Found by: BlueBison (code grep ws.go:421)
close_reason: Decided and partially built in ecdd831. DECODING: compressed messages are inflated for the operator's view where the handshake agreed no_context_takeover for that direction (core/websocket_deflate.go). EDITING compressed messages is deliberately REFUSED, not omitted: RFC 7692 s7.1.1 lets the LZ77 window carry across messages, so re-compressing only the edited ones corrupts every LATER message on the connection. Where decoding is not provably correct the message stays compressed and the note names the missing parameter, because a fresh window yields convincing WRONG plaintext on a surface read as evidence. Reopen if editing compressed frames is actually wanted; that is a whole-direction recompress, not a patch.

The React UI cannot select them: internal/web/ui/src/pages/matchreplace.tsx:19-27 (TARGETS) and internal/web/ui/src/lib/types.policy.ts:17-24 (MatchReplaceTarget union) omit both values. Fix is a two-line-per-value dropdown + union edit adding 'Request parameter name' and 'Request parameter value', then one manual check that a param rule survives the settings round trip.

title: burp-re: triage the 88 Montoya API types with no recorded implementation
description:
SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md §4 records that only 194 of 282 Montoya API types resolve to an implementing class via out/structural/montoya_impls.tsv. 88 resolve to nothing.

Those 88 are currently indistinguishable between two very different states: (a) genuinely internal-only, where Burp exposes the interface but implements it through a path the bridge did not capture, or (b) an incomplete bridge, where the implementing class IS in out/clean/jdt_src/burp/ and montoya_impls.tsv simply missed the row.

This matters because a parity audit reading 'no impl' will conclude 'Burp does this internally, we cannot compare' when in fact the code is sitting in the tree. That is a false negative in the oracle, and false negatives in the oracle become wrong gaps in burpsy-go/gaps.md.

Do: for each of the 88, search jdt_src for a class whose method set matches the interface (the specs in out/specs/md/ list implements/extends per class, so a signature-level join is possible without reading bodies). Classify each as internal-only / bridge-gap / ambiguous, and for bridge-gaps append the row to out/structural/montoya_impls.tsv and rebuild out/montoya_api/ with tools/build_montoya_index.py.

Evidence rules are in SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md §6: a guessed class name is worse than UNKNOWN.
close_reason:
Triaged all 88. Verdict: montoya_impls.tsv was NOT incomplete — exactly one real bridge gap existed (persistence.PersistedList) and it was an index-parser artifact, not a missed row.

Findings by category (evidence per row in out/structural/unresolved88-triage.tsv):
- 58 enums: implementation IS the constant list (e.g. core.ToolType, 15 constants, verified via javap); consumed by obfuscated code (HighlightColor 34 jdt_src files). No impl expected.
- 4 API exceptions (PromptException, MalformedRequestException, JsonParseException, ProcessExecutionException): thrown, not implemented.
- 1 internal locator (internal.ObjectFactoryLocator): static factory wiring, referenced by Zczq.java/Zsly.java.
- 22 extension-implemented SPI callbacks: javadoc prose says 'Extensions can implement this interface and then call X.register...'; registration methods exist in API-METHODS.tsv; obfuscated consumers verified in jdt_src (e.g. ActiveScanCheck/PassiveScanCheck 12 files each; Scanner impl Zemw.java consumes both). Zero internal implementors is CORRECT for these — the implementation lives in extensions.
- 2 vestigial API types (scanner.CrawlAndAudit, scanner.ScanConfiguration): declared in out/structural/hierarchy.tsv rows 20389/20393 but 0 consumers tree-wide and no shipped-2026.7 API method takes either; Scanner surface uses CrawlConfiguration/AuditConfiguration. These are dead API surface, not parity gaps.
- 1 parser artifact: h1 title 'Interface PersistedList< T >' — regex (\S+) stopped at the space, yielding FQCN 'burp.api.montoya.persistence.PersistedList<' which joined to nothing. Fixed in tools/build_montoya_index.py (identifier-only capture, not \S+); index rebuilt 2026-09-03: 282/282 types parsed, invariant ok, linked 194->195, unresolved 88->87. The 9 real implementors (Zbvx Zby5 Zez_ Zp0v Zpgl Zrip Zs0w Zw9w Zx9v, all also implementing burp.Proxyable) now appear in IMPL-BRIDGE.tsv.

Also fixed en route (found by the doc-audit subagent, verified against the tree):
- SOURCE-OF-TRUTH.md L96 'byte-identical to pristine' was FALSE: 764/19,309 files differ (fresh diff -rq re-run 2026-09-03: 630 record->class rewrites, 98 explicit '= null' initializers, 33 '[resugared]' constructor repairs, 4 '[unrecoverable]' placeholder defaults, 0 duplicate-interface removals; overlap partition 630/97/32/1/4). This also resolves the §10 'jdt_src is misnamed/provenance unknown' question: jdt_src = pristine + one repair pass, mtime 5 min later.

title: extender: no BApp Store and no Java/Python/Ruby (Montoya) extension model — plugins are local JSON-RPC executables only
description:
## Burp-side evidence

A Burp user's entire BApp ecosystem and Montoya extensions cannot be loaded. [DECISION] architecture/licensing call.

Type: Basic / NTLMv1 / NTLMv2 / Negotiate / Digest"). NTLM/Negotiate are needed for Windows-integrated and Kerberos-protected targets, a common enterprise case.

[DECISION] Adding NTLM/NTLMv2/Negotiate needs a sender/architecture change (per-connection auth affinity, Kerberos credential handling) — a product/architecture call.

title: session: rules cannot be reordered, so precedence between overlapping rules is uncontrollable
description:
## Burp-side evidence
settings/sessions/index.html: "By creating multiple rules, you can define a hierarchy of behavior... Every time Burp makes an outgoing request, it determines which of the defined rules should apply... and then performs all of the relevant actions in order." Macros: "You can also edit your existing macros, or change their position in the list."

## burpsy-side evidence
session.tsx rule list (650-696) renders each rule with only Enable/Edit/Delete; there are no move-up/move-down controls (contrast StepCard 372-382, which does have them for macro steps). SectionHeading (633-635) states "the first that applies owns the recovery" — so order is significant — yet a rule's position cannot be changed, so precedence between two overlapping rules cannot be controlled without deleting and recreating.
close_reason:
Implemented end to end: session rules can now be reordered, so precedence between overlapping rules is controllable.

Backend — Coordinator.MoveRule(id, offset) (internal/session/session.go, next to AllRules): moves a rule within the evaluation order slice by a signed offset, returns the new position. Design points, all documented in the code: (1) Moving is the ONLY way precedence could change and it is deliberately separate from UpdateRule, which 'keeps its identity (ID and position in the evaluation order)' — the old workaround, delete + re-add, minted a fresh id and broke every saved /api/session/rules/{id}/run reference while silently inverting precedence. (2) Signed offset rather than absolute index: a concurrent AddRule/RemoveRule between the operator loading the table and clicking shifts the rule relative to its neighbours instead of swapping it with whatever now sits at the target index. (3) Refusals, not clamps: a move past either end returns the new sentinel ErrRuleAtEdge (400 naming the edge) instead of a silent success that changed nothing; unknown id is ErrNoSuchRule (404). offset 0 is a no-op read reporting the current position. MatchingRule walks the same order slice, so the moved rule's precedence takes effect immediately and the id is never renumbered.

API — POST /api/session/rules/{id}/move with {"offset": -1|+1|N} (internal/web/api_session.go: sessionRuleMove, dispatched in handleSessionRuleDetail alongside the existing /update-macro and /run suffix routes). Answers {"position": N}; 404 unknown rule; 400 edge-refusal with the edge named; 405 with Allow: POST for other methods. Order is persisted immediately via persistSessionRules(), so a restart restores the moved rule at its new position (the restore path calls RestoreRule in persisted order — precedence survives restarts).

UI — session.tsx: up/down ArrowUp/ArrowDown IconButtons on each rule row (edge-disabled), calling new hook useMoveSessionRule (data.policy.ts) which POSTs the move and invalidates the session query so the table always shows the live evaluation order. New useMoveSessionRule hook documented with the 400/404 contract.

Tests — 11 new, all full-sentence claims per package convention:
internal/session/move_test.go (6): move swaps adjacent rules and MatchingRule hands the host to the moved rule; down-move updates position (second,first,third order asserted); moves past either edge are refused NOT clamped and refused moves change nothing; unknown id = ErrNoSuchRule; offset 0 is a positional read; the id is stable across the move (the delete+re-add hazard).
internal/web/session_move_api_test.go (5): wire round trip flips matcher ownership (allow_all scopes make position the only decider); unknown rule 404; past-the-top 400 whose body names the edge; GET on /move 405 with Allow: POST; persisted order after the move starts with the moved rule (AllRules is what SaveSessionRules writes).

Gate — go build ./... clean; go vet ./... clean; gofmt -l . empty; go test ./... all ok (including 167 UI checks via bun run check, 0 fail); UI bundle rebuilt (bun run build) since it is go:embed-ed. e2e: QUICK=1 e2e-go.sh = 20 passed / 4 failed, IDENTICAL on the clean HEAD baseline via git stash — the 4 failures (history path/status capture) pre-exist on this branch and are unrelated to session rules; no regression from this change.

title: organizer: no free-text search and no tool/parameter/file-extension/annotation filters — only scope, status class and MIME
description:
## Burp-side evidence
`tools/organizer/filter.html` — the Organizer filter window and search bar offer:

responses; requests with parameters; MIME type; status code; **tool**; **search term** (literal or

search bar.

## burpsy-side evidence
burpsy's Organizer exposes only three filter dimensions and no free-text search box. The filter state
is `burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/organizer.tsx:116-118`:
  `inScopeOnly`, `statusClass`, `mimeFilter` — and the toolbar at `:411-466` renders exactly those
three controls (In scope only / Status / MIME type) plus a Clear-filters button. There is no `<Input>`

title: logger: capture filter is tool-only — no capture-by-scope/MIME/status/search-term and no memory or size limit
description:
## Burp-side evidence
`tools/logger/filter/capture.html` — the Logger capture filter (Settings mode) has these dimensions:
"Capture limit [memory]... Capture by request type: Capture only in-scope items / Discard items
without responses / Capture only parameterized requests. Capture by MIME type... Capture by status
code... Capture by tool... Capture by search term (Regex / Case sensitive / Negative search)...
Session handling... Limit request/response size." The capture filter is destructive and separate from
the view filter: "Items that are not captured will be discarded from Logger."

## burpsy-side evidence
burpsy's capture axis is TOOL-ONLY. The UI renders one checkbox per tool and nothing else:
`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/pages/logger.tsx:320-335` (the `capture-axis` toolbar maps `tools` to
per-tool `<Checkbox>` only). The endpoint takes only `{tool, on}`:
`burpsy-go/internal/web/api_toolkit.go:903` `toolLogSetCaptureReq{ Tool string; On bool }` and
`:922` `s.toolLog.SetCapturing(tool, req.On)`. There is no capture-by-scope, capture-by-MIME,
capture-by-status, capture-by-search-term, no session-handling toggle, and no configurable memory or
per-item size limit (eviction is a fixed cap surfaced only as the read-only `dropped` count at
logger.tsx:255). So an operator cannot restrict what Logger records except by whole tool.
(Method/status/search filters at logger.tsx:84-102 are client-side DISPLAY filters over already-kept
rows — they do not stop capture.)

title: decoder: no Octal or Binary encode/decode function
description:
## Burp-side evidence
`tools/decoder.html` lists the encode/decode functions Decoder offers:
"The following decode and encode functions are available: URL. HTML. Base64. ASCII hex. Hex. Octal. Binary. GZIP."
Octal and Binary are first-class Decoder functions (e.g. decode `\101\102` or a binary bit string).

## burpsy-side evidence
burpsy's Decoder offers neither. The full transform vocabulary is fixed in the UI at
`burpsy-go/internal/web/ui/src/lib/data.workbench.ts:52`
  `DECODE_LAYERS = ["url","html","base64","base64url","hex","gzip","deflate","jwt","ascii"]`
and `:66` `ENCODE_ENCODINGS = ["url","html","base64","base64url","hex","gzip","deflate","ascii","rot13"]`.
The backend agrees: `burpsy-go/internal/tools/codec.go:48`
  `layerNames = [...]string{"url","html","base64","base64url","hex","gzip","deflate","jwt"}`.
No "octal" or "binary" case exists in `ParseLayer` / the encode switch, so the two functions are
unreachable from both the menu and the wire. (burpsy adds base64url/deflate/jwt/rot13 that Burp lacks,
but octal and binary are genuine one-way gaps.)
close_reason: duplicate of burpsy-react-ui-ku62 (created by a fork that re-ran this cluster; canonical bead kept)

title: intruder: no redirection handling — the attack never follows a 3xx and there is no Follow-redirections setting, so a result only visible after a redirect is missed
description:
## Burp-side evidence
tools/intruder/configure-attack/settings.html (Redirections) — Intruder attack settings include "Follow redirections" (Never / On-site only / In-scope only / Always) and "Process cookies in redirections", so an attack can chase a 3xx to the page that actually carries the result.

## burpsy-side evidence
internal/intruder/intruder.go:27-31 states the engine "does not follow redirects at all" and that the redirect config field was deliberately removed. internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx exposes no redirect setting. A login/brute-force attack whose success is only observable after a 302 sees only the 302.

[DECISION] burpsy removed redirect-following on purpose for scope-safety (per-hop re-authorisation through the scope chokepoint). Reaching Burp parity needs a product/architecture call on whether to reintroduce scoped redirect-following.

title: intruder: no 'URL-encode these characters' payload encoding — the default final-pass character encoding of the Payloads panel is absent, only a whole-payload encode processing rule exists
description:
## Burp-side evidence
tools/intruder/configure-attack/payload-types.html (Payload encoding) — the Payloads side panel ends with "URL-encode these characters", a box naming the characters Intruder URL-encodes in every generated payload as the final step before sending, independent of the payload type. Burp defaults this to characters like `=&?+;/%` etc.

## burpsy-side evidence
internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx has no payload-encoding control. Encoding is reachable only as an ordered processing rule (PAYLOAD_RULES "encode" with a layer, types.tools.ts:30, intruder.tsx:1274-1304), which URL-encodes the entire payload rather than a chosen character set and does not run as an automatic final pass. The default "URL-encode these characters" safety net is absent.

title: intruder: results table lacks Time-of-day, Cookies, Comment and a Timeout column distinct from Error — a result cannot be annotated and a timeout looks like any error
description:
## Burp-side evidence
tools/intruder/results/viewing-results.html lists the results-table columns: Request, Position, Payload, Status code, Time of day, Response received, Response completed, Error, Timeout, Length, Cookies, Comment. "Time of day - The time of day the request was made"; "Timeout - Whether a timeout occurred"; "Cookies - Any cookies received in the response"; "Comment - Any user-applied comment".

## burpsy-side evidence
internal/web/ui/src/pages/intruder.tsx:468 fixes the Attempts columns to: #, Payload, Status, Length, Time, Reflected, Grep, Error, Response. There is no Time-of-day column, no Cookies column, no per-row Comment column, and no Timeout column distinct from Error (intruder.tsx:468-497). A finding cannot be annotated in the results, and a timeout is indistinguishable from any other network error.

title: ui: table columns cannot be reordered by drag (no columnOrder in VirtualTable)
